utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly address you regarding the war diary, Exhibit Z610.1. According to Rule 89(C), the Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. It is settled law at the Tribunal that proof of authenticity is not a separate threshold requirement for the admissibility of documentary evidence. As regards hearsay evidence, it is settled practice of this Tribunal that relevant out of court statements which are considered by the Trial Chamber to be probative are generally admissible on the Rule 89(C). A piece of evidence is not admissible if it is so lacking in terms of indicia of reliability that it is not probative. Matters going to authenticity and whether a document is an accurate reflection of the events are matters for the Trial Chamber to assess when considering the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence. The issue raised by the appellant essentially goes to the determination of the reliability of this document, Z610.1, and whether the Trial Chamber abused its discretion when it assessed it to be sufficiently reliable to be admitted into evidence. The Prosecution submits that the appellant's arguments regarding admissibility and weight of the exhibit were fully litigated at trial and rejected by the Trial Chamber. In its decision of 1 December 2000, to admit Exhibit Z610.1, the Trial Chamber considered as relevant factors the unavailability of the exhibit during the presentation of the Prosecution's case, the cumulative effects of the material and whether the admission was in the interests of justice. This, according to the Trial Chamber's test, which it had formulated with regard to the so-called Zagreb documents on 21st November 2000. The Trial Chamber found that it was admissible, Exhibit Z610.1, because it was relevant to issues of the case and was contemporaneously made. You will find the Trial Chamber's specific considerations with regard to Z610.1 at paragraph 44 of the decision of 1st December 2000. utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'll respond to the appellant Kordic's argument on two issues: The arguments he raises in respect of count 1 of the indictment, persecution; and secondly, the issues he's raised in respect of the existence of and classification of the armed conflict in Central Bosnia. But first persecution. Your Honours, I could begin by pointing out that the arguments the appellant has raised in challenging his persecution conviction are overwhelmingly an attempt to simply re-argue the evidence from trial. But there is an even more fundamental point to address. If you consider Mr. Kordic's persecution arguments in their totality, it's clear that there are some fundamental misconceptions about the crime of persecution that underpin them. To illustrate what I mean, let me give you an overview of some of the points that he's made during this appeal proceedings. For example, in his corrected Appeal Brief of 12 July 2002, at page 76, he states that the conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia did not involve any more discrimination against or persecution of one community by another than is normally to be found in the turbulence of ethnic politics and the prosecution of a civil war once politics fails. Another example from the same brief, at page 94, where he describes the Croat treatment of Muslims in Busovaca as a far cry from the deliberate, calculated policies of persecution that the Serbs pursued against both communities. And further, his corrected supplemental appellant's brief of 4 March 2004, at page 33, paragraph 55, suggesting that if the ABiH was on the offensive, this tended directly to rebut any suggestion that it was the Croats who were persecuting the Muslims; rather, the reverse was true. Consider also, Your Honours, the appellant's repeated assertion that he is not guilty of persecution because there was no unilateral campaign. In essence, Your Honours, Mr. Kordic is asking you to do the following: He asks you to accept that the prohibition against persecution is relative, that some persecution is allowed, indeed expected in indeed all wars, and that the international community should not concern itself with that. He asks you to accept that if the parties to a conflict commit persecutory acts against each other, then that extinguishes the persecution in question, that unless a persecution campaign is one-sided, it's not persecution at all. And he asks Your Honours to accept that persecution is a label that should only be attached to the Bosnian Serbs because their behaviour, he suggests, is far worse. None of these propositions is correct. The prohibition against persecution is absolute. The label of persecution doesn't serve the purpose of issuing a judgement about which ethnic group committed the highest percentage of atrocities in the conflict, or indeed which ethnic group was the most defenceless. It's not a label that's applied to vindicate the political policies of one or other party to the conflict. It's a criminal law norm applied to protect individuals from having their rights violated deliberately, on discriminatory grounds, and to ensure justice to those individuals who suffer such violations. The fact that Mr. Kordic has been convicted of persecution is by no means a denunciation of the Bosnian Croat people as a whole; rather, it is about holding accountable one individual for his conduct that led to violating the rights of the Bosnian Muslim victims of the Lasva Valley and Kiseljak. Turning, then, to some of the specific arguments that Mr. Kordic has repeated from trial. He has denied that the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB, had a secessionist agenda. The Trial Chamber rejected this argument, paragraph 491, after fully considering it, and found that the HZ HB did indeed intend to secede from Bosnia and enter a union with Croatia. And Your Honours, it's little wonder that the Trial Chamber rejected the testimony of the Defence witnesses to the contrary, which the appellant has attempted to re-argue on appeal. The appellant has raised, in a bid to dismiss the Trial Chamber's reliance on Exhibit Z2717A, the minutes of the presidential meeting held by Tudjman on 27 December 1991. He claims that it's not probative, that it does not direct the use of force in pursuit of the territorial aims of Herceg-Bosna. Well, certainly, Your Honours, in December 1991, Bosnia was just beginning to splinter, and what we see at this meeting are the seeds of a plan that would be nurtured over the next two years. That is what the remainder of the evidence in this case was about. But this document warrants much greater examination than the appellant's cursory treatment. Ignac Kostroman, the secretary of the HZ HB, was present at that meeting in Zagreb. His intervention that day recorded at page 13 of the transcript, makes it crystal clear that the HZ HB was established to provide a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia. The argument that the HZ HB had no territorial aspirations has been put on behalf of Mr. Kordic by his lawyers. But I ask Your Honours to consider the actual words of Mr. Kordic at that meeting. He said: "The Croatian people in the region, the subregion of Travnik, live with the idea of acceding to the Croatian state, and they are ready to do so at all costs. The young men are teeming with Croatian spirit. I say this because I come from the field. We have visited every single village in the territory of the subregional community of Herceg-Bosna." At this meeting, President Tudjman also underscored his belief that the existing borders of Croatia were unworkable. Your Honours, why does it matter so much whether or not the HZ HB aspired to territorial acquisition and union with Croatia? And why has Mr. Kordic so strenuously denied it, even in the face of incontrovertible evidence to the contrary? Ask yourselves, Your Honours: How likely was it that the HZ HB's territorial aspiration could have been achieved when across the coveted territories there was a sizeable Muslim population? In many areas, the Croats had only a relative or very slim absolute majority. I refer you to paragraph 494, 499, 504, and 505 of the trial judgement in that regard. So although the aspiration was clear, the practical problem remained: How could the objectives of the HZ HB be achieved when almost half of the population in the key areas were Muslim? The evidence at trial, accepted by the Trial Chamber, revealed the tragic answer to that question. When it became apparent that the Muslims would not voluntarily accede to these territorial aspirations, the Bosnian Croat leadership, through the instruments of the HZ HB and the HVO, embarked on a step-by-step process aimed at confining and then eliminating, by violent means, all resistance from the Bosnian Muslims. They sought to subjugate them, to bring them under Bosnian Croat control. Mr. Kordic was the senior HDZ politician in Central Bosnia. He was the president of the HDZ in Busovaca and a member of the four-person presidency of the HZ HB, one of its two vice-presidents. So the reason why Mr. Kordic has denied the truth about the territorial aspirations of the HZ HB, even in the face of insurmountable evidence to the contrary is clear. When Your Honours understand the political backdrop to the events in this case and the location of Mr. Kordic squarely in the middle of them, it is a very relevant lens through which to view the events unleashed in Central Bosnia from 1992 onwards. Let me take Your Honours to paragraph 473H of the judgement. Consider for a moment the scene at the municipal hall in Busovaca in January 1992. Dario Kordic took centre stage in front of a cheering crowd that was chanting "Croatia, Croatia," over and over again. What did Mr. Kordic tell the crowd in the course of his speech that day in January 1992? He said: "I wish all of us the best with respect to the Independent State of Croatia." He said: "This is Croatian land, and that is how it will be." Then Ignac Kostroman, the secretary of the HZ HB, took the stage, and this is what he said to the cheering crowd: "We will be an integral part of our dear state of Croatia, by hook or by crook." And then he said something very telling. He said: "As for the remaining population in our areas, the question is asked: What about the Muslims? What about the Serbs and everyone else? Well, we can say to them: Let them not worry about everything. Let them live in our state of Croatia, and no one will miss even a hair on their head, if they accept us as their brothers and accept the fact that they will be citizens of the state of Croatia." And indeed, as 1992 progressed, it must have seemed to the Bosnian Croat leadership that the Muslims were not going to present a significant impediment. As set out in the judgement at paragraphs 494 to 520, starting with Busovaca in May 1992, the HVO progressively took over, municipality by municipality; oaths of allegiance to the HVO and the HZ HB were administered; the flags were hoisted over the public buildings; and the Croatian dinar was introduced into circulation. Violent acts against the Muslim population, designed to threaten and intimidate them, escalated as the year drew to a close. In the Trial Chamber's words at paragraph 537, by December 1992, the situation in Central Bosnia was this: The HVO had taken control of the municipalities of the Lasva Valley and had met only significant resistance in Novi Travnik and Ahmici. Much of Central Bosnia was, therefore, in the hands of the HVO. What we saw from January, after the ultimatum issued by the HVO, was the unleashing of a campaign of attacks targeted at the Muslim civilian population and designed to eliminate the resistance that had by that stage been demonstrated. The Trial Chamber found, in paragraph 827, that the underlying acts of persecution were attacking towns and villages with a concomitant destruction and plunder, killing, injuring, and detaining Bosnian Muslims. Mr. Kordic suggests that these acts were not the result of a persecutory campaign, just the unfortunate fallout of a war in which the HVO was seeking to achieve legitimate military objectives. Your Honour, there is one fundamental point to be recognised in this case: The agenda of the HVO in Central Bosnia was not just a territorial acquisition. It was to seize territory with a Muslim population so substantially reduced and subjugated that it would present no meaningful opposition to the union with Croatia, and it is the action taken by the HVO in pursuit of that illegal objective that underpins Mr. Kordic's conviction. My colleague Ms. Brady will take you through the events that happened in the various towns and villages, but let me make a general point about Mr. Kordic's argument of collateral damage. Collateral damage is, by its very nature, non-discerning and uncontrolled in its impact. Collateral damage does not discriminate between ethnic groups. It cannot distinguish a Croat civilian from a Muslim civilian, a Croat house from a Muslim house. Yet Mr. Kordic does not explain why, over and over again, in the villages under consideration, the death and property destruction caused by the HVO operations was surgically confined to Muslim civilians and Muslim houses. The appellant then seeks to explain away the crimes that were indisputably committed in Ahmici on the basis that they were not part of a persecution campaign but merely ad hoc war crimes. In effect, he tries to take Ahmici out of Central Bosnia, to remove it from the early morning hours of 16 April 1993. Let me take you to paragraph 613 of the trial judgement. The order to attack Ahmici, which was issued by Colonel Blaskic, commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, was an order to ethnically cleanse. Colonel Blaskic ordered the HVO military police to kill all the men of military age, expel the Muslim civilians and burn down their houses. The crimes that happened in Ahmici were not the spontaneous initiative of unruly soldiers run amok. It was persecution ordered from the highest level of the HVO military command. Your Honours, if I could, I'd like to go into a closed session. I have discussed this with the registry previously and I understand I will need to have a complete closed session, because I would like to play some closed-session testimony from trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. Mr. Kordic has claimed that his discriminatory intent for persecution has not been proved, because there isn't any evidence that he ever used inflammatory language or expressed prejudicial views about the Bosnian Muslims. Well, even that is not strictly accurate. There is, for example, the testimony of a witness at trial, a journalist who met with Kordic and recalled him expressing his views on the threat of Islam and the notion of a corridor from Bosnia through to Turkey. That evidence was referred to in the Prosecution's closing trial brief at 436. But more fundamentally, Your Honours, Mr. Kordic's suggestion that he can't be convicted in the absence of evidence that he used ethnic slurs reflects a misunderstanding of the mens rea requirement for persecution. The relevant test clarified by the Appeals Chamber in Krnojelac at paragraph 185 is the deliberate intent to discriminate on one of the listed grounds, specifically, race, religion, or politics. The Krnojelac Appeals Chamber also used formulations such as: Because of the victim's membership in a group, or on account of their membership in a group. So it's clear that what's required is for the victim's membership in one of the designated groups to be the factor that propels the accused to violate their fundamental rights. What is not relevant is whether the accused is motivated by pure ethnic hatred, by a desire for money, for power, to save his job, to advance his career, or for any other motive. The Krnojelac Appeals Chamber confirmed at paragraph 102 that personal motive is irrelevant. To conclude, even if the only thing that Mr. Kordic had against the Bosnian Muslims was that they resided in large numbers on the territories he so desperately wanted to see annexed to Croatia, that they presented a barrier to his aspirations for Herceg-Bosna; that, Your Honours, is enough. In order to eliminate the resistance the Muslims posed, he enthusiastically contributed to the campaign to subjugate them by reason of nothing other than their membership in a particular political or religious group. That is enough to satisfy the mens rea requirement for persecution. Your Honours, I'll move very briefly in the few minutes I have remaining to the -- Mr. Kordic's fifth ground of appeal concerning definitions of armed conflict and international armed conflict. First, the question of whether there was at all relevant times a conflict in the areas we're talking about here. Mr. Kordic has argued that there was not, based on the premise that the Trial Chamber failed to find protracted violence before April 1993. However, the protracted violence threshold is relevant only for internal armed conflicts, not for international conflicts, such as the one under consideration in the present case. This is clear from the Tadic jurisdiction appeal decision. At paragraph 67, the Appeals Chamber said that the definition of armed conflict varies depending on whether it is an internal or an international armed conflict in question. At paragraph 70, the Chamber went on to set out the relevant tests. Clearly, by its very terms, the first alternative, a resort to armed force between states, is the threshold test for international armed conflicts. The second alternative, protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state, is the threshold test for internal armed conflict. For international conflict, all that is required is proof of the use of armed force between two or more states. There is no requirement that the conflict be of a particular intensity or duration. So, for example, the Celebici Trial Chamber at paragraph 208 stated that an international armed conflict is simply any difference arising between two states and leading to the intervention of members of the armed forces. It makes no difference how long the conflict lasts or how much slaughter takes place. In the present case, the Trial Chamber found that there was a conflict that was international in nature because of Croatia's involvement. That is a point that the appellant skipped over yesterday by simply asserting that this was not a case involving armed -- resort to armed force between states. But the Trial Chamber found that is exactly what it was. Alternatively, Your Honours, even if the protracted armed violence threshold is the relevant test in this case, it has been satisfied. The highest threshold of protracted armed violence applies to internal armed conflict to ensure that it is clearly distinguished from situations of mere civil unrest, to which the laws of armed conflict have no application. I refer again to the Celebici trial judgement at paragraph 184. But in this case, where we clearly have two organised military formations engaged in high-intensity combat operations in Novi Travnik, in October 1992, and in Busovaca in January 1993, these events can't be mistaken for mere civil unrest. There can be no doubt of the Tribunal's jurisdiction. The appellant referred to the testimony of Mr. Watters, who made the comment that prior to April, the conflicts between the parties had appeared as punch-ups in comparison to what happened before that. Your Honours, the witnesses -- the Witness Watters was actually making the point that the April 1993 conflict was different because of its coordinated scale up and down the Lasva Valley all at the same time. The fact that he made the comment that this was different to what happened prior doesn't render the military operations that the HVO and ABiH engaged in prior to that, beyond the definition of an armed conflict. Indeed, it's interesting to note that the appellant has never contested that there were military operations in Novi Travnik and in Busovaca involving conflict with the ABiH. Rather, he has focused his efforts on attempting to blame the ABiH for starting it. Very briefly on the arguments the appellant has made regarding the overall control test, which was the standard enunciated by the Tadic Appeals Chamber. Your Honours, it is settled jurisprudence of this Tribunal that the overall control test is the relevant test for determining when a prima facie internal conflict is internationalised by the involvement of a foreign state. It was confirmed in Aleksovski, at paragraph 147, and Celebici at paragraph 26. In both cases, the Appeals Chamber concluded there were no cogent reasons in the interest of justice to depart from the overall control standard. Mr. Kordic relies on a nullum crimen sine lege point to say that it should not be applied. But the point of the Tadic Appeals Chamber's analysis was that the overall control test is and always was at all relevant times the correct law. And indeed the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 126 to 127, considered a nullum crimen sine lege argument identical in all material respects to the one that the appellant raises here, and dismissed it as a misunderstanding of the Tadic jurisprudence. The Prosecution submits that Mr. Kordic's argument should be similarly dismissed. And very briefly, to conclude, Your Honours, the indictment point that he raised concerning the proper mode of pleading international armed conflict based on the Simic trial judgement. But what is important to note is that the Simic Trial Chamber also recognised that it was important to consider whether other forms of notification to the accused, such as the pre-trial brief, had made it clear to the intervening state was. In this case, the Prosecution's pre-trial brief most certainly did that, and I could refer you, for example, to paragraph 68 of the pre-trial brief, also the Prosecution's opening statement at page 15 and page 85 of the transcript, where it is also abundantly clear the intervening state was alleged to be Croatia. Indeed, in a motion hearing before the trial even started, on 16 February 1999, at page 530 to 531 of the transcript, the Defence acknowledged that they knew full well that it was the -- Croatia who was alleged to be the intervening state. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions. I will hand over to my colleague, Ms. Brady, unless there are some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you one question. It's about the time frame of the armed conflict and the international armed conflict. I take it, based on the -- please correct me if I'm wrong- I take it that both parties agree that it's undisputed that at least since April 1992 there was such an armed conflict. In paragraph 31 of the judgement, it reads: "Based upon the foregoing, the Chamber finds that, while it was not until April 1993 that a generalised state of armed conflict in the form of a protracted violence broke out in the territory of Central Bosnia. Between the HVO and ABiH, prior to that period, there were localised areas of conflict which a state of armed conflict could be said to exist." utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, our submission is that the international armed conflict, as analysed by the Trial Chamber in this part of the judgement that you refer to, extends back certainly to 1992. Some of the evidence that the Trial Chamber referred to was that of General Bobetko, who was a Croatian commander, who had been issuing various orders and setting up command posts and things of the like. So our submission is that the international classification of the conflict certainly relates to the entire indictment period, as the Trial Chamber indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning. Good, Your Honours. This morning I'll be responding to Kordic's arguments concerning all of the underlying counts of his convictions. This is counts 3 to 43. So, in a relatively short space of time, I'll be dealing with his arguments on his convictions for unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, murder, wilful killings, inhumane acts and inhuman treatment, imprisonment, unlawful confinement, wanton destruction and plunder, and if I get to it, destruction of religious institutions. Now, before I turn to what Mr. Smith called the core of his appeal, he began by making submissions on a very important point, and that is the question of the Trial Chamber's factual findings, and in particular, whether or not they can be properly supported, seen as properly supported in the judgement. I think it's important to distinguish between two types of factual findings that we see in the judgement. The first are the factual findings regarding the crime base, such as: Did wanton destruction take place in a particular location, like Stari Vitez or Vitez? Was plunder made out for Novi Travnik? Did killings occur in Nadioci, Santici, and Pirici? Then there are linkage factual findings, what Kordic did, his contributions, not just on every particular attack but even during the intervening periods, between the attacks, and these linkage factual findings can be found throughout the judgement and collectively, of course, form the legal basis for his liability under counts 3 to 43. If we look at the crime base factual findings, we can agree with Mr. Smith that the Trial Chamber did not, generally speaking, go through and do an element-by-element analysis, did not explicitly set out, rather, in the judgement, on an element-by-element basis, each of the underlying crimes in each of the 30 or so localities. What it did do, as Mr. Smith described, was to set out of the evidence of the parties and then follow it by what he called a conclusory paragraph of its findings, and he pointed out the example in paragraph 649. Your Honours, this style may not win the legal penmanship award. We don't quibble with that. But that's not the issue. The real question is whether this Chamber finds that those concluding factual findings are sustained on the record and for which the only inference is that the Trial Chamber must have accepted that evidence set out in the judgement before the concluding paragraph to reach that factual finding. Now, I can't go through each locality and each crime. We're talking about 20 or 30 locations and somewhere in the vicinity of between two and ten crimes, types of crimes, found for each. I think there must be at least 200 underlying crimes. But what I'll do is when I go to the core of his appeal, what I'll try to do is to try and highlight that, with possibly a few exceptions, the Trial Chamber's factual findings can all be supported on that basis. And in particular, Your Honours, you'll see several references in the judgement from which it can be clearly inferred that where the Trial Chamber did not reject evidence, it accepted it. And I point you to two matters in particular. If you look at the concluding factual findings on the crime base, such as paragraph 649, paragraph 800, and paragraph 808, what you'll see there, the Trial Chamber states that it rejects the Defence case and, importantly, finds that the crimes were committed as part of a pattern, the wider pattern of attacks. It's also very important to notice in the judgement that where the Trial Chamber rejects evidence, it states explicitly in the judgement that it does so, and we see several examples of that, such as when witnesses had given testimony about seeing Kordic on television saying certain things, the Trial Chamber was careful to say: No. We're not going to accept that evidence. And it's set out in the judgement. So from this, our submission is that the clear inference is that the Trial Chamber accepted the evidence which it set out in the judgement, sometimes it's in paragraphs and sometimes it's in the footnotes, except Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where it explicitly rejected it. And again, when I go through and talk about the factual findings on specific attacks and times, I'll try and show you some examples of this. Mr. Smith also mentioned and took issue with the Trial Chamber's factual findings that I mentioned, the second type of factual findings, those needed for the linkage to Mr. Kordic, and he said that the findings are imprecise, or they're inconclusive, such as pointing to the one in paragraph 586 about Busovaca, in which it was found that he was implicated in the attack as a leader, asserting political and military authority. And he similarly took issue with 631, 642, 669, and 726. Now, this is a critical question, because it's hinged on the way the appellant understands Kordic's legal liability for these counts 3 to 43. And in our submission, he's mischaracterised the true basis for his liability. It comes down to paragraph 834, where the Trial Chamber sets out its characterisation of Kordic's responsibility under counts 3 to 43. And it labels his responsibility as this: To plan, instigate, and order these crimes. What does this mean? What really is the legal basis for Kordic's liability for these crimes? And it's critical and has to be decided for your proper assessment of the linkage factual findings which are in the judgement. Mr. Smith said that the finding regarding these counts 3 to 43 is for his "direct participation, through planning, instigating, ordering, sometimes perhaps committing." In our submission, the true nature of Mr. Kordic's legal liability for counts 3 to 43 - and I want to get away for the moment from any legal labels and terminology - but the true reason is because of his participation, his very significant participation, in a common criminal plan, you could call it a common criminal design, you can call it a common criminal enterprise, and this was at the heart of the Trial Chamber's ascription to him of legal responsibility, and as such in this respect, the factual findings linking him to all the crimes of which he has been convicted are more than sufficient. It's an important point, so I'll just detail a little bit more about this basis for his liability. In our submission, it's clear that the Trial Chamber found that the criminal plan was this: To subjugate or remove the Bosnian Muslims of this region by various acts of mistreatment, by unlawfully attacking towns and villages, by destroying their property, by killing Bosnian Muslims and doing all the other various inhumane acts that we see strewn throughout the judgement. These were the core crimes of the common criminal design or plan to which he was a party. Now, within that common criminal plan or design or enterprise, Kordic played a multitude of roles, sometimes direct and sometimes what we could call indirect. We have to keep in mind that the Trial Chamber was looking at Kordic's contributions over a very long period of time, and his contribution wasn't a static one. It was a dynamic one. And we even see it's an evolving one. Sometimes he's participating very directly on the ground in Busovaca and Novi Travnik. Sometimes he's authorising or approving orders very directly, such as in Ahmici and the other mid-April attacks in Lasva Valley and Kiseljak. And sometimes he gave orders himself. Sometimes his role is best described as preparing. Most importantly, at all times, he's planning at a strategic or wider level. This conceptualisation of the true nature of his criminal liability and whether this be through joint criminal enterprise, normal principles, or through joint criminal enterprise combined with another mode of liability, not only reflects the facts in this case, but when you read the whole judgement, not just picking paragraphs out of context, if you look at the whole of the factual findings and especially the Trial Chamber's constant references to the criminal design or plan to which Kordic is a party, it's clearly the way the Trial Chamber viewed his liability. It would also be very odd if his persecution conviction, in paragraph 829, were hinged on this common criminal design, plan, or purpose, JCE-type principles, and yet the underlying crimes through which the persecution happened were not. In brief, his liability under counts 3 to 43 is centred on the common criminal plan and his significant contributions to that criminal plan or design, and whether he's ultimately been found to be a committer through a joint criminal enterprise or an orderer or a planner through a joint criminal enterprise, the most important point is this, as the Trial Chamber itself pointed out in paragraph 853: "He played his part as surely as the men who fired the guns." I'll turn back now to the core of his appeal. Responding to his arguments is not easy, for this reason: By discussing each attack, each municipality individually, the appellant has quite cleverly deconstructed the events. But in doing so, in our submission, he's in fact created a misleading characterisation of what actually happened. And what this Appeals Chamber should be especially cautious about is not to fall into the easy trap that this compartmentalized approach could invite. And just as the Trial Chamber did, you have to keep all of the connections and the relationship between all the facts and all the evidence firmly in mind. The Prosecution acknowledged at the outset this is a complex, circumstantial case, illuminated by occasional shafts of light of a direct nature. And when you review these convictions, never lose sight of the complex interrelationship of all the factual findings based on this truly voluminous amount of evidence, and whether it's of a direct or indirect nature, each fact, each piece of evidence, feeds into and informs the assessment of the others. It's like a thick cable of facts and evidence which led to his convictions. Yesterday the point was made in a different context about Judge Bennouna's comment on judicial or juridical impressionism. And it leads one to think: This case is a bit like an impressionist painting. When you stand really close to the painting, all you see is a bunch of dots. You don't see the image. But when you stand back a bit, the image starts to emerge. And when you see the whole picture, you have no doubt about what you see. And when this kaleidoscope of evidence is considered in its entirety, the only true picture which comes into focus is that which was found by the Trial Chamber. I note the time, Your Honours. Before going into each attack on individual basis, that may be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we have the break, I understand your point how to understand the judgement as such, but I would ask you, in particular, to focus on count 10 and 12, because there it seems to be a little bit more difficult, really, to find the factual findings of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Ms. Brady, before starting, may I draw your attention to one point when you are now discussing the counts through 43. I wonder about the mens rea underlying. We heard this morning that we should accept that there was an action based on joint criminal enterprise. However, maybe - and please correct me if I'm wrong - in your final trial brief, at paragraph 445, the Prosecution submits that Mr. Kordic is responsible under 7(1) for planning and ordering. Does it mean that your contribution of this morning, does it mean that you now waive your approach?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't waive our approach. We acknowledge that the Prosecution closing brief at 445 does make this reference, but we submit that it must be read in conjunction with paragraphs immediately above it, and in particular, paragraph 443 of the closing brief, in fact, in our submission envisages such a concept of principles of joint commission through jointly being part of a criminal design or plan. Your Honour, I just can't locate my copy of the portion of the closing brief. Just one moment. Excuse me. And, Your Honours, we can see that the Prosecution closing brief begins with an analysis of persecution in which it's stated that he's -- he should be liable as a co-perpetrator for the persecution. Then when we go to counts 3 to 4 and all the remaining ones up until 43, we noted in paragraph 443 that all of these crimes are constituent elements of the systematic pattern of victimisation of the Muslim population in Central Bosnia between November 1991 and March 1994, and accordingly are discussed together. Then when you go into the next paragraphs submitting that he be responsible for planning and ordering, in our submission, the only reasonable way to read it is as -- given that it's a joint crime involving so many people - of course he's not directly doing every single step. You can't just look at each attack and microscopically analyse was he ordering on this occasion. But our submission is that if you read it, the whole tenor is that he's part of a joint commission, a joint plan, a criminal plan, and that's the basis for his liability. And that's either a joint criminal enterprise through his own contributions in ordering and planning and instigating or that he's in fact ordering and planning through a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would stick finally to that what you said there, that, I quote and it's a quotation in itself: "Namely he directly or indirectly intended the crimes to be committed. Kordic either directly planned and ordered the crimes or accepted the risks that crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal would be committed as an ordinary result of his plans and orders dolus eventualis."

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission all of the corps -- all of the crimes all of the underlying crimes are actually corps crimes, if we look at it as a joint criminal enterprise, and they were all intended by the criminal design which was aimed ultimately at the further purpose to remove or subjugate the Bosnian Muslim population. But there may well be some crimes which possibly could fall outside that aimed at shared intention and then of course we're in the land of joint criminal enterprise category 3, and our submission is that his criminal responsibility then is for all crimes intended by that criminal design and any reasonably foreseeable ones of which he willingly accepted the risk. And I'm not sure if we call this a dolus eventualis or inadvertent recklessness. I realise that those terms come with their own specific understanding based on different criminal systems, but we would prefer to stick with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal on joint criminal enterprise category 3 and say that he was either aware of the risk -- sorry, he was aware of the risk and that he willingly took the risk or at least was indifferent towards that risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would in fact be your definition of dolus eventualis as opposed to direct intent or dolus directus?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move now to the individual attacks. And if I understand, we have approximately one hour to go through what is a voluminous set of crime base and factual findings on his responsibility. What I'll try and do is go through it on a chronological basis. Yesterday in argument Mr. Smith and Mr. Naumovski interchanged their arguments and didn't do it exactly in a chronological order, but in our submission, it is more logical to do it this way, and it's also very key, because out of this chronological pattern, we can see this emerging pattern and the role of Dario Kordic evermore clearly. Turning first to Novi Travnik, his conviction for wanton destruction and plunder during that week of 19 to 26 October. The primary or the first question he asks is: How could this be war crimes when it was just normal fighting during a civil war and not part of a persecutory campaign? Firstly, his hermetically or his analysis of the fighting in Novi Travnik in this vacuum, this hermetically sealed vacuum which he divorces from all the other facts which my colleague Ms. Jarvis mentioned this morning and which could be found in paragraph 511 of the existing persecutory campaign in Novi Travnik and the other Central Bosnian municipalities since the 1992 takeovers. It's not only artificial to separate it, it's actually wrong. And the Trial Chamber was more than entitled to consider that background, that persecutory background, when considering whether what took place then was simply destruction in the course of a normal war or, as the Trial Chamber found, war crimes, namely wanton destruction and plunder. Now, he says that -- or Mr. Smith said, argued that certain key elements, certain key factual findings are missing from the Trial Chamber's analysis here on wanton destruction and plunder. Looking at the witnesses' evidence of the extensive and deliberate destruction of Muslim-owned houses, businesses, restaurants, in our submission this cannot be considered anything but destruction on a large scale which was not justified by military necessity. How could it be as he calls it expectable collateral damage when you have witnesses like C, Witness C, at transcript 796 to 800 who described how the structures in residential areas and some distance actually behind the front line were set on fire and demolished? And bringing it back to his point that he made about the lack of concrete findings regarding lack of military necessity. Not just for Novi Travnik, but it's equally applicable for all the villages we see. In village after village we see the same deliberate burning, the same torching of houses. Sometimes the soldiers have gasoline pumps attached and are spraying it and then setting it afire. How could this be urgent and required for the attainment of a known military purpose to burn down houses? It's beyond explanation, and in our submission, the factual findings on this point for Novi Travnik, as in other places, is quite safe. And in terms of plunder, surely witnesses like Ismet Halilovic's description of HVO soldiers stealing people's cars must satisfy the unlawful appropriation needed for plunder in view of the clear absence of circumstances rendering the appropriation lawful under international law such as contemplated by The Hague regulations. He also asked yesterday what about sufficient ministry value? Well, for a start, with plunder it has -- it's not just looked at from an individual point of view. It's looked at also as Celebici Trial Chamber notes from an overall effect as well. And again, what I'm saying about plunder in Novi Travnik is equally transportable when you look at the findings on plunder, on lootings in the other locations. The findings don't evaporate at all. On the second point he raises for Novi Travnik, he asks why is Kordic liable for the criminal acts done by the other HVO soldiers? Factually, we know from the Trial Chamber's judgement that it's because of the leading role he played in the fighting. How could this be an unreasonable finding? True, it was Colonel Stewart's first day on the ground in Central Bosnia, but let's not forget he's an experienced military commander, and when he formed the impression of Kordic being an effective military commander, this was based on his own direct observations, how Kordic was interacting with the other soldiers, how Stewart negotiated with Kordic himself. I also draw Your Honours' attention to the very telling military reports, and they're summarised at paragraph 528. For example, in Exhibit Z243, the CBOZ report over the names of Blaskic and Kordic. This was spoken about yesterday. "While Defence operations are being conducted, Dario Kordic and I are in Novi Travnik continuously leading the military operations with deep knowledge of the situation and keeping all forces under control." See also Exhibit Z249, a co-report by Blaskic and Kordic on the 24th of October relating directly to the Novi Travnik military operations. The Trial Chamber also didn't overlook other very important facts Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. showing by this stage, by this time he had clear political and military authorities which this crystallized. They found this, for example, from his role in the Ahmici barricade incident. At the same time, 19th to the 20th of October, 1992. And even from what he -- from his leading role, leading the HVO delegation at the mixed military working groups just a month later. In our submission, there's -- the Trial Chamber was quite correct to ascribe him with responsibility under 7(1) for the HVO soldiers' criminal acts either under the principles of common criminal design which we say by that stage had crystallized, or even on a more direct basis as the evidence clearly satisfies. Turning to Busovaca in January of 1993, his argument was that the ABiH began the fighting and any HVO reaction were just normal military ones and not part of a campaign of persecution. Again be very careful with how he removes Busovaca. He takes it away from the rest of -- from its context. And in our submission, from the entirety of the evidence, the finding at paragraph 576 that the attack on Busovaca was the beginning of a pattern of attacks designed to remove or subjugate the Muslim population was the only reasonable conclusion. And again Busovaca has to be viewed in light of what had been going on there since the takeovers in 1992. I won't deal with all the evidentiary issues that he raised or the arguments concerning some of the evidence, but just on a few more of the salient ones. He mentioned Witness AS's evidence. This was the fourth military police insider. It's true. AS said the HVO military police were never ordered to direct offensive operations against civilians or burn Muslim houses, but it's difficult to see when AS himself agreed with the Prosecution's description of this attack as a cleansing operation to see how he could have understood this to mean a normal military cleansing or cleaning or clearing operation. It's very difficult to understand that interpretation when in re-examination Witness AS, at T16437, agreed with the Prosecution's description that it was an ethnic cleansing operation. In any event, just as all the evidence in this case, AS is just one piece of the complex circumstantial cable of evidence that the Trial Chamber relied on to find that what took place in Busovaca in January of 1993. It wasn't just simply collateral consequences of a legitimately fought civil war but was, in fact, the beginning of this pattern of unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects followed by the killings and other inhumane acts, wanton destruction, and plunder. And most probative on the situation for Busovaca is the witnesses' descriptions themselves. In particular, I invite Your Honours to look at Witness J, transcript 4524 to 29, and AG at transcript 14138 to 39. These witnesses spoke of what we might call the signature details which we see time and again in the later HVO attacks in April and June. Early morning shelling and sniping, blowing up and setting fire to Muslim houses, shops, restaurants, and widespread looting of houses by the soldiers. When considered alongside the January letter, the ultimatum letter, the only reasonable conclusion is that this attack was either deliberately aimed at civilians and civilian objects or, at the very least, was indiscriminate in failing to discriminate between civilians and military objectives. And his attempt to recharacterise this as a normal military operation with just sort of unfortunate but expectable collateral consequences is factually unsustainable. As for his point about Blaskic being stuck in Kiseljak when it commenced, I think that this actually, maybe unwittingly, perhaps to further highlight the point because Kordic was in control of the situation. On his second argument about Busovaca, why is he legally liable for the soldiers' criminal acts in Busovaca; factually, the Trial Chamber premised it on the fact that he played a leading role in exerting his effective military authority in the attack. Now, I can't possibly re-argue nor should I the whole case, the whole evidence in the case, but there's no other reasonable interpretation which is open other than at Busovaca he had this very active military role. Look at what the international witnesses like Major Jennings and Colonel Stewart thought about him, describing his role as effectively a military commander there. Look, too, at the tape recording that was mentioned yesterday, the tape recording of the phone call between Blaskic and Kordic on the 23rd to 24th of January, 1993, and summarised in paragraph 577. Now, he can now try to reduce its import and say, well, this is just a sort of meddling in military activities or a joke or bravado, but these arguments were rejected by the Trial Chamber, and I suggest its proper reading shows exactly why it was so rejected. And in that phone call, Kordic in fact orders Blaskic to fire at Kacuni, telling him to burn everything. I also invite Your Honours to look at him giving military commands such as exhibit Z421.4 where he's actually ordering an HVO brigade on the 30th of January, 1993, to send a company to Busovaca to carry out combat activity. He says that he can't know or doesn't know on what basis he bears 7(3) possibility for Busovaca. It's because of this: By January 1993, he was part of a common criminal plan or design to subject the Muslim people of Central Bosnia to a variety of unlawful acts and mistreatment so as to subjugate or remove them from the area, and in this respect, we can't forget that by this stage he was the most influential political leader in the region, not to mention having this significant input into military matters. And in our submission, what happened in Busovaca, all the unlawful attacks fell squarely within that common plan or design or at least were reasonably foreseeable and ones that he ran the risk, willingly ran the risk. I'd like to turn to the question that he raised about a possible inconsistent finding, and it relates to the inconsistency of findings in paragraph 576, that there were no unlawful attacks on Merdani, and yet the Trial Chamber found wanton destruction for the purposes of count 38. If we look at Witness A's description at transcript 354 to 56 of the shelling that Merdani suffered, and when we look at it combined, in combination with the video made by Mr. Capelle, the one from the helicopter, which showed the clear destruction to this civilian village. In our submission, this is sufficient for a finding under wanton destruction. If anything, in our submission the Trial Chamber could also have convicted him under counts 3 to 4, the evidence showing a clearly unlawful attack that day, deliberate, or at the very least indiscriminate. So if there is any error which arises from this inconsistency, it's inured to the accused's benefit. Yesterday, Mr. Smith said that there was a generalised -- he said there is a general submission, lack of findings for the count 4, attacks against civilian -- unlawful attacks against civilian objects, and there was a general lack ever finding that the damage or destruction to civilian objects was extensive. Now, of course, the notion of extensiveness of damage to civilian objects, it's difficult to define with great precision. However, in our submission, for Merdani just as for the other villages there were ample findings and ample references to evidence in the judgement to support that element for wanton destruction. I'll turn now to the mid-April attacks in the Lasva Valley. My colleague Ms. Jarvis this morning mentioned that his treatment of Ahmici has to be very carefully reviewed. He now admits that what happened in Ahmici was a clear case of war crimes. He calls them ad hoc war crimes, in no way capable to the attacks happening simultaneously in the villages up and down the Lasva Valley, as if it were some kind of aberration. This point has to be completely disavowed. Yes, Ahmici was the high point. Yes, it suffered the worst out of all of the villages. But to see the attacks on all the Lasva Valley villages in April, and we're speaking of a distance, I think, from Busovaca to Kiseljak of 25 kilometres, to see it as anything but an orchestrated and connected pattern of events would be completely unreasonable. Now, my colleague Mr. Farrell yesterday already addressed you about his main argument on Ahmici, and it was hinged on AT's testimony. If you accept the findings in 631 that it was reasonable to conclude, based on AT's evidence, on Blaskic's orders on the 15th and 16th of April, all the facts regarding Blaskic's and Kordic's working relationship, we could call it, if you accept on the basis of all that that it was reasonable that Kordic was present at the meeting of politicians on the 15th of April at which the attack to cleanse Ahmici and the other Lasva villages was planned and at which Blaskic's illegal order to kill all the military men, expel the civilians and set the houses on fire was approved, then of course you don't need to go any further to find that what happened on the 16th of April in Ahmici were war crimes and persecution, and his criminal responsibility flows from that. But the point was stressed yesterday, and I want to make it again because it's important when we come to look at the other attacks. AT's evidence, of course it's very important, but it's not the only evidence of the existence of the criminal design or plan upon which the entire case, whether it's Ahmici or the other ones, rises or falls. Instead, the focus always has to be on the pattern of events unfolding simultaneously through the Lasva Valley in over 20, 25 different localities between 16 and 18 April. Was it just a coincidence that the same pattern of attacks, the early morning shelling and sniping on Muslim only or Muslim majority villages, taken by surprise, Croat neighbours having been forewarned before in many of them, killing people in often house-to-house raids, sniping civilians, setting fire to their houses and businesses, stealing their personal property like jewellery, TVs, refrigerators. Was this just all a coincidence that happened up and down the valley at once in legitimate military operations? And this goes to the heart of his argument when he said that the Trial Chamber merely just found HVO military attacks on villages. No, it didn't. It found much more than that. It found an orchestration of attacks by the HVO, an orchestration that was clearly aimed at an illegal purpose. In his brief he didn't go through it so much yesterday, but he did make a point in his brief that I would like to come back to. At times in his brief he implied that some of the international witnesses may have countenanced the possibility that what happened along the Lasva Valley can be explained by FIBUA, fighting in built-up area techniques. Now, international witnesses like Stewart and Bowers, yes, they acknowledge the existence of this technique, but in fact they rejected the idea that the destruction such as occurred in the various places, Ahmici and all of the other places, could be explained by that. For example, for Ahmici, Colonel Stewart dismissed it out of hand because of the systematic and surgical nature of the destruction and, for example, the use of snipers to cut off escape routes for civilians who were trying to flee. I'll turn now to the grouping of villages Nadioci, Pirici and Santici, and I'll deal with the sufficiency of factual findings and at the same time try to address the Pre-Appeal Judge's questions directed at the parties on the 29th of April as to the factual findings for killings and inhumane acts and inhuman treatment. Briefly in relation to the killings we note in particular reference to footnote 1241 and especially exhibits Z1583. These are death certificates of people who were killed in Ahmici and the associated hamlets on the 16th and 17th of April showing 28 people who died in Santici, 16 in Pirici, and 3 in Nadioci. For inhumane acts and inhuman treatment here, for Pirici we note exhibit Z1583 -- sorry, excuse me, we note exhibit Z1594.3, which is

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Ms. Enes Hrustanovic born in Pirici. We note that Nura Pezer at T15449 to 50 describes her husband as badly injured and then shot and killed by the HVO there. And finally for Nadioci we note the testimony of S at T7941 to 42, who testified about a woman detained and raped at the Bungalow in Nadioci. In our submission, these descriptions are legally sufficient to fulfil the elements of inhumane acts under Article 5 and inhuman treatment under Article 2 either by mounting to serious physical or mental suffering or injury or at the very least serious attacks on human dignity. At this point, if I could try and address the question posed by Judge Schomburg relating to how these particular counts fit within the joint analysis through joint criminal enterprise. In our submission, the inhumane acts in its various forms committed against the civilians would all fall within the common core JC 1 centre of the criminal design. At the very least, they would fall within those, if we think about category JCE 3 within those that were reasonably foreseeable and for which he willingly ran the risk. Now, turning to his arguments on the three hamlets from Ahmici, again he says -- again he says that any harm done was simply expectable collateral damage during legitimate fighting in a built-up war, and points out that those were both strategically located and defended. Again, these pattern -- these attacks on Nadioci, Santici, and Pirici were part of the simultaneous pattern of attacks by the HVO involving the same types of clearly criminal conduct, clearly unlawful behaviour in the conduct of hostilities. Besides, what military objective is he saying was the target here? He can't just say oh, well, the whole village or one of the villages was on a useful road and therefore I can use whatever means, even illegal ones, to take it. It has to be shown that there was a legitimate military object and a lawful means of achieving it, and unlawful means such as indiscriminately bombarding a whole village or deliberately sniping and shooting at civilians or burning down houses, it can't be sanctioned obviously because a village is on a good road and useful for communications and transport. Regarding his argument about even if the illegal orders were issued in relation to Ahmici, this doesn't prove that they applied to the other locations or that he intended or foresaw that the crimes in the other locations would take place. Even if we were to adopt his very narrow reading of what the plan is or what the orders are, his argument begins, in our submission, on a false premise. As my colleague Mr. Farrell pointed out yesterday, the illegal orders were not just confined to Ahmici. We have to keep that in mind. If we look at the whole package of evidence, Blaskic's orders, for example, were directed to all units, and just take a look at the combat issue -- orders issued on 16th of April at 1.30 a.m., such as exhibit Z676 and exhibit D343. It's also important to bear in mind that the HVO representatives from each of the main municipalities that we're talking about here on the evidence of AT accepted the meeting which planned and authorised those illegal orders. We had Kordic, Ivan Santic, the president of Vitez HVO, Pero Skopljak, the chief of police in Vitez, Zoran Maric, the president of HVO Busovaca, and a representative from the HVO Novi Travnik. The argument also in our submission doesn't just begin on a false premise but it ends with a mischaracterisation, and it misses the key point. And from all the evidence, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to conclude by at least the eve of 15th of April 1993, and this was their finding in paragraph 642, there was a common criminal design involving Kordic to ethnically cleanse these villages and towns of Lasva Valley, and his liability for those crimes arises because, as a member of the JCE, indeed as a planner and an instigator of it -- in it, he intended those crimes to take place as a means to pursue the ultimate criminal goal or at the very least willingly ran the risk that they would occur as a reasonable -- as a foreseeable byproduct of this criminal plan. I won't dwell on Stari Vitez and Vitez. He was very brief on these villages yesterday. In the interests of time I'll move on to another set of villages. utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. You directed us and I'm very grateful for this in relation to Nadioci, Pirici, and Santici, to witnesses, to the testimony of witnesses, to exhibits, and so on, but where in the judgement do we find this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the judgement, when you look at footnote 14 -- no, sorry, 1241, we see reference to exhibit Z1594.3. That's the reference for what happened in Pirici.
