That's the highest I can put it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but to insist on this, you -- in the beginning, you highlighted that what was already discussed during trial, that it seems to be more or less a kind of a picture of impressionism, and we have to bring the bricks together. But would it, in your mind, be sufficient first to address certain acts in the footnote and then refer us to what is behind the footnote? Is it sufficient for a judgement in criminal matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our submission, based on what I said in my earlier part of my submissions, this is the technique which is used here. I said that perhaps it -- we would wish for better legal clarity to join up every piece of evidence that was relied on for a particular fact, but that doesn't mean that when you come to review, what you're basically doing is not so much to catch out whether there are difficulties with the Trial Chamber but whether a conviction is safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll turn briefly to Donja Veceriska and Gacice. He didn't mention these yesterday, but I'd just like to make a few points in passing because they are important for this proper view of the whole -- the whole pattern. And in this respect, Your Honours, I point to what happened in Donja Veceriska -- the description of what happened in Donja Veceriska at 645 where Witness V gives the description of what happened when, after the shelling began at 5.30 with the anti-aircraft gun shooting from the factory nearby, and then grenades were thrown into the houses and the residents and others were arrested and beaten and then the majority of Muslim houses were burned and people were killed and the village was destroyed by explosives and fire. Does this strategic position on the up-slope of a hill overlooking the Vitezit factory change things? No, it doesn't sanction HVO soldiers to bombard them by using this indiscriminate shelling and firing, throwing grenades into people's houses and firing deliberately at civilians. It doesn't justify the murder of local civilian inhabitants, burning down their houses and stealing their valuables. We would think as well that if it was so strategic, one would expect that an army would want to keep it as much intact as possible. I also want to mention that in relation to all the what we will call the non-Ahmici villages, we can't forget that the Trial Chamber had other very important evidence corroborating not just the existence of the common criminal plan but indeed Kordic's active engagement with it. For example, my colleague Mr. Farrell pointed out that he was seen with Kraljevic in the Vitezovi barracks pouring over a map and discussing military matters, and it makes no difference if this was on the 15th or the 16th of April. We also point out the VBOZ duty officer's logbook which my colleague Ms. Kind mentioned, and it records ten phone calls between Blaskic and Kordic on the 16th of April, starting at 9.00 in the morning until 7.00 at night, 7.30 at night discussing the details of the military operations. And Ms. Jarvis mentioned the very telling one at 1802 where Kordic is telling Blaskic, Pasko has finished it off and is pressing on. He didn't mention the villages of Loncari and Ocehnici. I won't address on those, and I'll move now to Rotilj and the other Kiseljak villages in April and then in June of 1993. You'll know from the map that this area of Kiseljak, the villages of Gomionica, Svinjarevo, Gromiljak and the others, this is only some 25 kilometres down the valley. So in fact what's happened is the action, this pattern of attacks has moved down here. I'll deal first with the issue he raised yesterday about the sufficiency of factual findings on this point, and in our submission, it's clear that when you read the last sentence of paragraph 809 which, at the Status Conference on the 6th of May, all parties agreed that this last sentence should in effect be read as a separate -- like a separate paragraph, when you read that together with paragraph 808, it's clear that the findings there apply to the previous facts which had been set out by the Trial Chamber in the preceding paragraphs 805 to 808. Now, we do recognise his -- that he's pointed out that the reference to Kiseljak municipality is omitted in 809. I can't explain this by any other means except to say that if you read the whole of that chapter 6 and in light of paragraph 806 and 808 in particular and then 834, this has to be a clear drafting error, and I can't explain it any more than that. I'll deal now with Naumovski -- Mr. Naumovski's argument. What Mr. Naumovski failed to say when he discussed these attacks in April and June is that what happened in these villages mirrored what happened in the other places. If we look at paragraph 665 and footnote 1327, the pattern of destruction almost follows a script. Svinjarevo, houses set on fire, mosque burnt down, Croat houses remaining intact. Gomionica, shelled by HVO, plundered, houses set on fire. The list goes on. He can't -- his argument that Rotilj was a militarily strategic place, how can this justify what happened when the evidence actually discloses that the TO was asked to surrender the guns before the HVO shelled the village and then the houses and barns were set on fire? How could it ever make the burning down of houses in all these villages as being somehow justified by military necessity? Now, his main argument, of course, on this was the link to Kordic, and in our submission, the Trial Chamber was quite correct to link these attacks on Kiseljak villages in mid-April as part of the larger pattern of attacks and falling within the scope of the criminal design to which Mr. Kordic was a party. And it's not inconsistent with the finding that the Trial Chamber found before, that he had no real control over Kiseljak. It's not about that. It's about the scope of the criminal design. And we can see that the Trial Chamber has made this finding. If we look at 669, again it's not like they disassociate themselves with all the other evidence, but in particular here they're looking at the close temporal and geographic proximity to the Lasva Valley attacks, Blaskic's orders, Z733, when it says we're keeping the very top or the top or just the leadership of the HZ HB informed, and particularly this symbiotic, entwined relationship between Kordic and Blaskic. Just look at the frequency of their discussions on military matters from the 16th through to the 20th of April. No wonder the Trial Chamber found that Blaskic would not have launched the attacks without Kordic's approval and that Kordic was associated with them. Finally, I'll turn to the attacks on Tulica and Han Ploca on the 12th and 13th of June. This two months after the mid-April attacks and this time the action has moved a bit further down the valley. Again mirroring the previous attacks Tulica an all-Muslim village in the midst of Croat villages. The hallmark features again, heavy shelling; HVO soldiers setting houses on fire; applying gasoline through pumps or sprays, killings, women being forced to give up money and jewellery, survivors rounded up for detention. Likewise Han Ploca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry could you please guide us to the paragraph or footnote in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm referring to paragraph 721 for Tulica, and paragraph 722 for Han Ploca and footnotes accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: In our submission, no error arises in finding that these attacks were part of this orchestrated and sustained HVO attacks. And as for the link to Kordic, well, Mr. Naumovski, he didn't mention the real link via the common criminal plan. Instead, he focused on the Trial Chamber's reference to Witness Y seeing Kordic in the Kiseljak barracks as if it's all based on that. But that's not why Mr. Kordic is linked to these June crimes in Kiseljak. It isn't did Mr. Kordic's singular involvement in the day-to-day operation of the attack of one particular attack that makes him liable. It's not about basing this part of his conviction as one person being in one place at one time. It's for his role in the common criminal design or plan, the plan of which he was an integral member of. And so for that reason, there is no error in the Trial Chamber's finding that he was associated with the giving of orders to attack these places and thus liable. In the two minutes remaining, I'll turn extremely briefly to detention crimes. Not much was said on these. In fact, Mr. Smith said that he was resting on his brief on this point, but I want to turn briefly to his challenge as to the sufficiency of findings as to detainees being civilians or protected persons, and in this respect, I draw Your Honours' attention to basically all of the findings, all of the summary evidence, 774, 777, 780, 81, 783, 790 to 92. And on this evidence of Muslims who had been arrested, rounded up, and taken to detention centres following, immediately following the attacks, the Trial Chamber's find information paragraph 800 become clear. The Trial Chamber wasn't wrong to reject his argument that the imprisonment of these Muslim civilians was not unlawful because they had been detained somehow for their own safety or their own security. The circumstances simply do not sustain any reasonable inferences but that this detention was indeed lawful. In fact, it's getting close to what the ICRC commentary rejects, this wholesale labelling of everyone from a certain political or ethnical background as a threat to security. Finally as to the link to Kordic, the Trial Chamber was not in error to find in 802 that this unlawful confinement was part of the common design to subjugate the Muslims. Let's remember it begins with the -- with the initial assault and then it ends, it culminates in detaining any surviving Muslims. We must look -- pay particular attention as the Trial Chamber did to the regularity, to the systematicity of this going on. And the Trial Chamber was not an in error to draw inferences from his position and activities as a political leader to find that he ordered and planned for the coming into existence of the detention centres in the areas in which he held responsibility, namely those in the Lasva Valley. And his argument yesterday that some of the Prosecution witnesses had agreed that he perhaps had no political authority outside of Busovaca is beside the point. It doesn't, as he puts it, eliminate the factual predicate for the detention findings for all but the Kaonik prison. The factual predicate is there. It's through the common design or the plan to which he was a major party. On sentencing, the Prosecution rests on its submissions in its brief, and just to reiterate, we would not take issue with some of the matters such as family circumstances may as a matter of law be mitigating, just as the Kunarac Appeals Chamber noted that. But just as in Kunarac, the question is: Is error shown in the exercise of discretion in giving no weight to such circumstances when compared to the seriousness and the gravity of crimes? And just as in Kunarac, we would submit there would be no reason to mitigate his sentence on this basis or any of the factors he puts forward as mitigating. Your Honours, that concludes the Prosecution's case except for the one point that Her Honour Judge Weinberg de Roca raised about the -- whether the authenticity of three documents had been challenged in other cases. If I can with your indulgence, the Prosecution is looking into this matter and will get back to you as soon as we have that information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you for all your contributions, and let's dedicate now the next 30 minutes for the -- yes, it was planned already earlier, I know -- the reply for the Kordic Defence. And my apologies to the Defence of Mr. Cerkez. However, it will facilitate maybe your submissions if you only start after the lunch break. So please, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And to answer Judge Weinberg de Roca's question, Exhibit Z1380.4 and Exhibit 1406.1 were so-called Zagreb documents which made a very late appearance in the Kordic case. They were not exhibits in any other case. Listening to the Prosecution's submissions, I must say that I am minded of the description of -- given by Sir Percy Blakney of the Scarlet Pimpernel. We see him here. We see him there. We see him everywhere. Is he in a heaven or is he in hell? That darned elusive Pimpernel. And using another one of the images that the Prosecution used when you get very close to the facts in this case, it's like I think the phrase was a bunch of dots. And when you stand back, what do you see? What you see is a smaller bunch of dots. Unfortunately, there is no cohesive pattern, no way to fine your way through this convoluted and jumbled judgement which I regret to say omits significant factual findings as a predicate to the return of verdicts of guilty against our client here. This is not a matter of penmanship or poor legal penmanship. This is a matter of fair notice and a fair trial and, at its foundation, justice. The evidence in this case is indeed a kilometre wide, but consider when you look at the evidence and assess it, I think you will agree with the Kordic Defence that it's a millimetre deep as to Kordic, because the essence here is linkage. Where's the linkage between Mr. Kordic and these crimes? Where's the mens rea? We have some technical difficulties I regret to say. We have got a slide presentation. I see it's on the screen right now. My screen is not working here, so I'll read off my colleague's. Let's consider proposition by proposition in a sequential order starting with first counsel for the Prosecution and ending with last counsel for the Prosecution, what we heard yesterday and today. First, this was not a 7(3) case we're told. Well, the Appeals Chamber may well ask, did the Prosecution seek the imposition of a life sentence under Article 7(3)? And the answer to that question is yes. In fact, they vigorously pursued that in closing argument. So when did it cease to become a 7(3) case? Only when they lost it. Second proposition: Notice in a pre-trial brief can cure a defective indictment. It cannot for the reasons stated very recently in the Rasevic decision just two weeks ago. If the Defence is denied the material facts as to the nature of the accused's responsibility for the events pleaded until the pre-trial brief is filed, it is almost entirely incapacitated from conducting any meaningful investigation for trial until then, and that's exactly the case. And so let's take a look at the pre-trial brief that we got. What does it say? Paragraph 5: "Those committing such crimes may leave little documentary evidence. The Prosecutor may have limited access, if any, to other direct oral evidence of the commission of such crimes." Paragraph 6: "Accordingly this case is based in large measure on the proper inferences that can be drawn from the surrounding facts." Paragraph 12, and this is absolutely telling: "Difficulty in identifying a defendant's role may itself be indicative of guilt. In the absence of something to hide, there should be no reason for controversy about the true role of these defendants." And if you look at the evidence, there is no controversy about the true role of Mr. Kordic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What is a material fact? We know, because we agree with the Prosecution on that. The Prosecution tells us that a material fact as defined in the Kupreskic appeals judgement is a fact upon which the verdict is critically dependent. And is the verdict critically dependent on the version of events related by Witness AT right at the end of the case? Unquestionably it is. In terms of evolving law and the rights of access to closed-session testimony. That's not the point at all. The point is the right to a fair trial as the Tadic Appeals Chamber said so long ago. The right to a fair trial is central to the rule of law. It upholds due process of law. A proposition, of course, not lost upon the Prosecution which made an admission in this case that timely fulfilment of Rule 68 disclosure obligations is essential for a fair trial. Did we get access to General Blaskic's open-session or closed-session testimony? No. How do we know that? Take a look at the screen? The Prosecution accepts that Kordic was never granted access to Blaskic's trial testimony. We got it years and years later. Why? What changed? What made it exculpatory in 2003 and just a few months ago when it wasn't exculpatory throughout Mr. Kordic's trial? Could we use the testimony with open-session testimony, those parts of it that we did have without knowing what this witness had said in closed-session testimony? Of course we could not. And furthermore, it's absolutely integral in the jurisprudence relating to Rule 68 disclosure obligations that open-session testimony as well as closed-session testimony must be disclosed. Was it here? Absolutely not. We could hardly call General Blaskic to testify cold without knowing what this witness had said in closed session. We made attempts, as the Appeals Chamber knows, to interview this witness ourselves while the trial was under way. Those attempts were rejected by General Blaskic's counsel. The point is real made in the Krstic decision on subpoenas. You can't call someone without knowing what they're going to say because to do so would be contrary to the duty owed by counsel to their client to act skilfully and with loyalty. A point made expressly to the Prosecution in letters that we have attached to our supplemental reply brief filed in March of this year. I'll just put them -- there's a letter dated April the 10th. Would you take the chance of using open-session testimony if you could be decapitated by closed-session testimony? The question asked of the Prosecution. Of course not. And nor could we. And that's precisely the point made by Krstic. And the point was made again in a letter that's also attended to our supplemental reply brief, a letter dated later in the month.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- deliberate. There's no controversy about this proposition, Your Honours. The Prosecution admits it. Excuse to justify this. Well, we didn't think that the general was telling the truth, so we decided we weren't going to give it to Mr. Kordic. Now, what kind of an excuse is that? It's no excuse whatsoever. It's also been rejected as an excuse by the Blaskic Appeals Chamber as recently as two months ago in the 4th of March, 2004 decision because it's the credibility of evidence that falls to be considered in such circumstances by the Chamber, not by the Prosecution. It's not free to make subjective evaluations like this. It has a duty to disclose and it has to fulfil that duty under its own professional standards and under the jurisprudence of this -- this Tribunal. In connection with the credibility theory, I might point out this theory has been rejected by this Appeals Chamber in connection with Witness AT and the stories he told and whether he has recruited on his own initiative or not the individual who was recruited to produce perjured testimony in support of his alibi. Consider this hypothetical: In a murder Prosecution, Prosecution seeks the death sentence, yet it knows of an ironclad alibi. It contends nevertheless that the person who givers the accuse that had alibi isn't really to be believed so we're not going to turn that information over to the accused. Is that acceptable conduct in any jurisdiction, in any national jurisdiction, in the lowliest court of any national jurisdiction let alone in the most lofty court, this court. Absolutely not. That is unacceptable conduct anywhere. Was the general's testimony exculpatory? Well, you've just heard an extended recitation of the asserted military powers that our client supposedly exercised but let's take a look at the what the general said. The Prosecution recognises that Blaskic refutes the proposition that Kordic exercised any military control. Kordic personally was not in the chain of command. He Did not function within the chain of command between the military police and the battalion. He was with the civilian authorities. "In Novi Travnik, I was conducting all of the military operations there," said the general, yet he wasn't convicted and Kordic was. How? "Kordic was not within the framework of my command. He was not a member of my command. His statements were not binding upon me." In answer to an express question by Judge Jorda, "were you subordinated to Kordic in any way?" "No, Mr. President, I was not subordinated to him at all." Now, that's exculpatory and no credible argument could be made with a straight face that it is not; yet, what was told to the Trial Chamber? We've fulfilled all of our obligations and because we have, you should deny Kordic's motions for access to amongst other things the general's closed-session testimony. My word would be good enough I trust on this topic and if it isn't, I shall like to know why. Well, now we know why. That was on the 20th of January, 2000, two months before the close of the Prosecution's case. Eight months later, the same formula is recited and on both occasions this was relied upon by the Trial Chamber. If counsel gives me its word in court, that's good enough. Motion is denied. "Already dealt with and refused," says the court on the 3rd of August, 2000. "We've been told that the disclosure rules are being complied with and so that your motion your new motion is also refused." You've had full disclosure according to the rules we were told by the Presiding Judge. The real sense the Prosecution carries out its full duty under Rule 68. That's your safeguard. Well, it wasn't. And what's the Prosecution panacea for this violation? Well, it's very easy. All you have to do is ask for the admission of new evidence on appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Question by Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sayers. You have just said that your client, Mr. Kordic, didn't exert any military authority. Certainly the responsibility pursuant to Article 7 of the Statute can be attached to civilians as it can be to military men. It can refer to both if it is established that they had to power to prevent crimes or to punish others. Now, your client was a -- an eminent political figure. He was part -- or, rather, he was at the head of the leadership of local politics, and with the hypothesis that he had no authority to prevent crimes, did he not perhaps have a certain amount of authority which he could have wielded with the result that he could have taken the matter up and punished the perpetrators? So could you please indicate to us with the clearest cut lines whether he reacted in that direction, whether he acted in that manner at all during the material time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Guney, and that of course is the issue. That is the issue. Did he have the power of control? Did he have the power to punish? Did he have the power to prevent? Absolutely right. And I can answer your question, I hope, with some immediacy and some precision insofar as the inquiries that you make. If you turn to footnote 870, I think it's 870 -- I'm sorry, it's 973 of the judgement, this is a partial answer to one of your questions. Witness CW1 and the Appeals Chamber will be mindful of the lofty military position of this particular witness - by the way a Court witness, not called by either of the parties - said in evidence that Kordic had no power to initiate disciplinary action, and there was no evidence to contradict this. Secondly, if Your Honour turns to paragraphs 840 and 841 of the judgement, the Chamber finds in paragraph 840 that Kordic lacked effective control. And then in paragraph -- and the evidence we would submit is uncontroverted on that. And the second paragraph, 841, "Kordic was neither a commander nor a superior in respect of the HVO since he possessed neither the authority to prevent the crimes that were committed nor to punish the perpetrators of those crimes, and as such he is not liable under Article 7(3)." So there are the findings, actually clear findings, which is a rather unusual feature of this judgement. But more importantly, findings that are unappealed, unchallenged, by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have another question for you, Mr. Sayers. I should like to have your opinion or, rather, the Defence's point of view. He didn't have the power and authority to make decisions with respect to disciplinary action, and he did not have the effective power to control, lacked effective control, and if he didn't have the power to prevent either, were there nevertheless certain cases in which and above all with the sightings with -- to his high position, did he not have the power to prevent or, rather, if he did have the power to -- did not have the power to prevent, he could have wielded his authority vested in him to have a certain amount of authority to follow up and punish the perpetrators of crimes as well as the perpetrators of atrocities committed. So would you agree with me there, that although one does not have the power to prevent, one can wield one's authority and follow cases up and punish the perpetrators, at least to take steps and initiate certain mechanisms, to put into motion certain mechanisms to do so and to investigate and punish? What is the point of view of the Defence on -- in that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That question, of course, Judge Guney, is, to use a colloquialism from where I come from, that's where the rubber meets the road. Does this man have the power to initiate disciplinary proceedings? Does this man have the power to punish de facto as opposed to de jure, and the answer to both of the those questions is: Absolutely he did not. The testimony from the HVO military witnesses top to bottom is uniform and consistent from the chiefs of the Main Staff of the HVO, several of whom testified before the Trial Chamber and whose evidence is before this Chamber. General Blaskic's second in command Major General Filip Filipovic testified Kordic walls not in the chain of command. He had no power over any of our subordinate brigades. He had no power to issue orders to Blaskic to initiate discipline action. He had no influence over the military police. That testimony is confirmed by General Blaskic's Chief of Staff, Brigadier Nakic, by other staff officers such as major Prskalo, Brigadier Gelic; by brigade commanders such as Zivko Totic, Neven Maric, Vinko Tokic, Dusko Grubesic. It's also confirmed ironically by two commanders of the military police, the 4th battalion of military police. I went over that testimony yesterday with colonel Palavra. It's the same for Ljubicic's predecessor Colonel Zvonko Vukovic. Kordic was not in the chain of command. So the evidence is quite clear and it's not contested by the Prosecution although there's a certain distance between that, the failure to appeal the acquittal on Article 7(3) and the argument that the sentence should -- should go northwards. But point is there's no evidence that this man was in the chain of command, that he had the power to punish, that he had the power to prevent and those are the express findings in the paragraphs and footnote I've just recited of the Trial Chamber and those findings are precise and they're unchallenged. I had various other points to make, but my time is short here. I want to finish on this note before I hand over very briefly to Mr. Smith who will have a word to say on persecution. Mens rea. That's where it comes down to. That's exactly what the question is about. We understand that, and the Appeals Chamber understands that. And here it is. Here's what the state of the art is. Krstic just a month ago. There must have known formula in the blast zone of responsibility, so to speak, he was close enough, associated with, implicated in. Essentially a guilt by association argument. Is that enough in this Tribunal? It is not. The Trial Chamber's assertion was without approve evidentiary basis said the Krstic Appeals Chamber and this Appeals Chamber should say the same thing without having established that Krstic knew of the intention on the part of General Mladic, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made the further inference that Krstic shared that intention. And finally in the Vasiljevic appeals judgement earlier in the year, without proof of the appellant's intent, the appellant would not be responsible as a co-perpetrator in the joint criminal enterprise. And where is it? He's everywhere and nowhere, just like the Scarlet Pimpernel. This case is no more than a bunch of dots. It's exactly juridical impressionism, exactly what Judge Bennouna called it several years ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to discuss very briefly essentially five points relating to persecution and counts 3 through 43. The first relates to the alleged deconstruction by Kordic of the evidence in this case. This argument reminds me of the Heisenberg principle. This argument and the shift into an argument that it really is all a joint criminal enterprise and individual proof of ordering, planning, instigating, or committing is not necessary for the count 3 to 43 events. You know the electron is in that cloud someplace. You know that the linkage, it is asserted, is in that cloud someplace in the atom, but you can never put your finger on its location and its time at any point. The second point I want to make is as to Kordic's responsibility and the basis for that responsibility under Article 7(1), that is to say paragraph 834 of the opinion relating to counts 3 through 43. The Prosecution is at this late stage in the case attempting to rewrite what the Trial Chamber said -- Trial Chamber said. The Trial Chamber clearly found liability under Article 7(1) for planning, instigating, or ordering, and while it used -- referred to the evidence relating to persecution, it clearly did not make a finding under joint criminal enterprise. And the Prosecution has suggested that we simply sweep aside the legal terminology. But you can't sweep aside the legal terminology. The legal terminology is the way lawyers discuss with precision what is the meaning of the legal conclusions they're reaching to convict a person of an offence and put him in gaol. The Prosecution now argues that joint criminal enterprise can be combined with joint commission, co-perpetratorship under Article 7(1) for the offence of planning, instigating, or ordering, but these are two entirely separate concepts. The Prosecution also suggests that having attempted to take counts 3 through 43 and wrap them in the common plan, that almost everything that is in the case is in the common plan because that's what's alleged under counts 3 through 43, but just in case there's anything that they've forgotten, there's actually a category 3 intent rather than category 1 intent because of a joint criminal enterprise and everything else is reasonably foreseeable. Your Honours, this is a form of confusion. This takes us back to the amended indictment which was not precise, to judgement which was not precise, and now neither Kordic nor the Appeals Chamber can tell what the Prosecution really thinks about the critical linkage issues, and that this new importation of joint criminal enterprise into the findings for counts 3 through 43 is yet another example of the Prosecution's case simply moving and shifting wherever it thinks it needs to go to get to the predetermined conclusion that it wishes the Appeals Chamber to head toward. The third point I will make is the Prosecution asserts that the citing of a sentence out of Mr. Kordic's briefs that Kordic takes the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. position that you can have a little persecution. That is a misreading of our brief, Your Honour. We quoted, put in quotes the words "persecution" and "discrimination" in that sentence because we did not intend them to be taken literally as the Prosecution has done. The point we made and have made continually is that where there is conflict, military or political, between two groups, political groups, religious groups, racial groups, by definition to some extent one group is always opposing the other group, members of the other group, because they are members of that other group. That is the only point we made. My fourth point, Your Honour, is that the Prosecution has argued that collateral damage does not distinguish between people and houses, but the Appeals Chamber must take what the Trial Chamber did not take, and that is a realistic view of what happens in military combat. Muslim houses were frequently destroyed because that's where people were shooting from in a combat situation. Where there is evidence that they were destroyed later, you must look carefully to see whether there was such evidence and whether it was clear that the destruction was not related to the combat. And I will take just several examples of where you must look carefully at the evidence. Donja Veceriska. They fought for 48 hours until the Muslim, the ABiH ran out of ammunition. You must look very carefully, because we do not believe that it is clear from either the judgement or the opinion that there were civilians killed there. And on the detention offences. Those detentions took place during periods of active combat, active fighting, and it is not just a matter of protecting the civilians, but it is also a question of military security. My final point, Your Honour, and that is as to the secessionist agenda. I refer Your Honours to pages A41 through 48 in the annex to our trial brief where we have discussed at length the question of secession, the question of the Tudjman papers in particular and who said what, and you will see there that Mr. Kordic was talking about the existence of the Croat community within the RBiH. That's the essence. With that, Your Honour, I will close, simply saying that where, as in this case, you are dealing with political and military events involving persons of different religious or political communities, you must apply the concepts of the law carefully and particularly the concepts of persecution carefully. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I finally ask, you didn't answer to the point made by Ms. Jarvis that the Prosecution submitted that the HVO operations were surgically directed to Muslim civilians and Muslim houses. Would you agree with this? And you made just two minutes ago the point, what about the targets of the attacks? Would you agree with the submission of -- by the Prosecution that the target of the attacks were civilian and civilian objectives?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is our assertion that in the bulk of the situations involved, the attacks were against legitimate military objectives, and we have tried to spell out why each village made sense as a military matter, as a point of attack. And there were many villages that were not attacked. And secondly, we assert that as it is necessary that the fighting was not directed at civilians or civilian objects, it was a military engagement. The question then becomes, because of course during a military engagement there are likely to be collateral impacts, were those collateral impacts excessive? Where there is evidence that civilians were killed, that's the question. Were there more civilians killed than is warranted by the nature of the fighting in this built-up area in each village. Where houses are involved, you must ask yourself whether there is clear evidence that these houses were destroyed by fire or some other manner not related to the combat, and clearly attributable to HVO soldiers and the evidence in Novi Travnik does not clearly attribute the destruction of property to HVO soldiers. The evidence simply is property was destroyed, some of it outside the area of the fighting. You must look at the findings with care, because sometimes there may have been deliberate destruction of houses, but you must look very carefully and ask yourself these questions, and in most cases it was legitimate military objectives, and we assert that it was acceptable collateral damage and these attacks were directed as military matters, not as against civilians and their houses per se, with the clear exception of Ahmici. That's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes this morning's session. We will have now the break until a quarter to two sharp. The trial stays adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was informed that the Prosecution wanted to answer a question put to the Prosecution this morning by Judge Weinberg de Roca. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. This concludes now the hearing on the appeal lodged by Mr. Kordic, and as we have to deal with individual criminal responsibility, we have to turn now explicitly and solely to the appeal lodged by Mr. Cerkez. And no doubt we are fully aware that some additional time has to be allocated to you, and my suggestion would be that if you need all the time, we can continue right now until a quarter past 3.00, and then half past 3.00 till 5.00. And let's see whether you can finalise your submissions in this time allocated to you. The floor is yours, Mr. Kovacic. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I also hope that we will be able to present what we have planned within that time allocated to us. As a matter of fact, we tried to organise our arguments within three hours, which is the amount of time that was originally allocated to us in Scheduling Order. It doesn't matter whether those three hours would begin today at 11.00 in the morning or just now, at 2.00 p.m. By way of introduction, I would like to mention several elements of historic nature in this case, because I think that this has accompanied the case from the very beginning and gave a negative connotations. As you know, the amended indictment was -- original indictment was issued on the 2nd of November, 1995, against six persons initially: Kordic, Blaskic, Cerkez, Aleksovski, Skopljak, and Santic. The Prosecution first dropped charges against Santic and Skopljak, whereas later on the case against Blaskic was severed from the case against Aleksovski. Together with the indictment in the Kupreskic case, four new cases, all having to do with the Lasva Valley, were established before this Tribunal. Cerkez learned of this indictment later on. He prepared for his defence to a certain extent. He came to the conclusion there was no need to hide, and voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal. That was on the 5th of October, 1997, and since that time, he has been in detention here. During his first Initial Appearance in October of 1997, Cerkez pleaded not guilty with respect to the crimes he was charged with. The amended indictment charged Cerkez with 22 counts. The trial judgement found him guilty of 15 counts and acquitted him on 7 counts. Perhaps it would be easier if I presented a chart to you now, which gives the information pertaining to locations and the temporal scope of the indictment. I will revert back to these issues later on. The indictment shows, and you can see it from this chart, that the relevant time of the indictment goes from the 1st of April 1992 to the 30th of September, 1993. However, the most significant counts in the indictment are all limited to April of 1993. The second feature of this indictment is the geographical scope. This indictment charges Cerkez with acts committed in municipalities, so not in towns but in municipalities, which is a much broader term, the following municipalities, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, and Vitez. The judgement, in the end, reading the findings and not only the ruling of the judgement, one sees that Cerkez was convicted only for the events in the territory of Vitez municipality and, to be more precise, in an even more limited area, precisely three locations within that municipality. Therefore, from a very broad geographical scope that we had in the beginning, Cerkez was found guilty for acts committed exclusively within his municipality, or rather, in the town where he lived and in the vicinity of that town. The next feature of the indictment is a crime which took place in the Ahmici village on the 16th of April, 1994. I wish to say the following regarding the scope of this: Cerkez has been acquitted of all charges concerning the incident in Ahmici. Therefore, acquitted of all charges concerning the acts which took place in Ahmici. The second matter that needs to be mentioned is that, regardless of the fact that other villages were mentioned within that area near Ahmici, namely, Nadioci, Santici, and so on, I would like to say that during the very lengthy trial that we had, we established a practice whereby all of these four sublocations - Nadioci, Pirici, Santici, and Ahmici - are referred to under the general term "Ahmici." As a matter of fact, it is one location, and it is very difficult to discern one from another. We think that when formulating the indictment, the Prosecution needlessly divided the territory into these four hamlets, these four sublocations. I still wish to remind you that Cerkez was convicted for Prosecution under Article 7(1), as a co-perpetrator, and was convicted for other acts he was found guilty of, which is counts 3 to 44, and his criminal accountability was established both under Article 7(1) and under Article 7(3). We will revert to that later on, because we believe that cumulative charging under Article 7(1) and 7(3) is permissible; however, cumulative convictions under both of these articles is not in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The jurisprudence after the trial judgement was passed down. I would like to state for the record that, in addition to this, Cerkez was found guilty under count 35 and count 44. However, during appeal proceedings, the Prosecution stated that it believed that these two counts were errors, or erroneously entered into the judgement, and therefore, the Prosecution was of the opinion that these two counts need not be discussed now. I would like to state now that as far as count 44 is concerned, which pertains to destruction of religious -- of buildings dedicated to religion, in the Prosecutor's brief and response under paragraph 1067 -- 10.67, to be more precise, stated that they believed that the Trial Chamber made an error and that Cerkez should be acquitted under Article 7(1) of the Statute for count 44 because there was no evidence to substantiate that he was involved in the destruction of the mosque. And then they go on to give details, but we need not go into that. The Prosecution might say something about this matter. As for the other counts, count 35, the Prosecution dropped this charge several days ago in their submission -- in their filing on the 14th of May. Therefore, there is no need for me to spend time on that issue. However, if you should find it necessary, I'm prepared to discuss this as well. Next, I wish to remind that the pre-trial proceedings lasted 18 months. During that time, the Trial Chamber reviewed about 60 various motions of the parties, meaning that all parties were very active during that phase of proceedings. The Defence, among other things, also asked, on the 22nd of January, 1999, that the indictment be formulated in more specific terms. That motion of the Defence was denied, as was the practice in all other cases at the time. The Prosecution said to us today, or perhaps yesterday, in the afternoon, that the indictment was made more specific by adding two additional documents. One was mentioned as being their pre-trial brief, and the second one was this so-called annex 1, which accompanied either that brief or the indictment; I cannot remember exactly. However, it is our position that the indictment remained fairly vague. We will discuss this a bit more later. The indictment was definitely too broad, and these added documents, which were supposed to make the indictment more specific, did not actually provide additional clarifications or accurate facts. As a result of that, the Defence spent a lot of time defending our client from charges that we were not even sure that he needed to be defended for, and the Defence was never quite clear on the scope of the indictment. I'm sure that the Appeals Chamber will take this into account when formulating their decision. As you know, the trial itself lasted for 244 trial days, 244 witnesses were heard during trial by all three parties. There were two witnesses who were summoned here by the Chamber. In addition, 30 transcripts relating to 30 witnesses from other trials were admitted as well. Those were mostly witnesses from Blaskic and Kupreskic. And in addition to that, 49 affidavits were admitted, in accordance with the Rules which were in force then, and the Rules have been changed in the meantime. 4.665 exhibits were admitted and, in the end, the transcript amounted to almost 29.000 pages. Following the judgement, additional disclosure, under Article 68, continued -- under Rule 68 continued, based on our records, the Prosecutor has lately disclosed to us more than 70.000 pages of new material. What should be borne in mind is that the new material was disclosed to us under Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Rule 68 and that most of that material came from the military archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence asked to be given access to those archives during trial, and the Chamber granted these two requests on the 27th of January and on the 6th of July, 2000, and ordered the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to disclose the requested documents to the Defence. However, this did not materialise, despite the promises given by representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence was given only 27 documents, and I have to tell you that those were absolutely worthless documents. I don't think that any of the Defence counsel used it in their defence case. These documents did not pertain either to the temporal scope or to the events that were discussed here during the trial. Later on, we were told that the Prosecution informed us that we would be granted an agreed -- we would be granted a chance to review these documents in an agreed manner; however, I have to say that this did not happen, despite the fact that the Prosecution had full cooperation of various organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina pertaining to their cases in Lasva Valley. They never, in fact, tried to establish the location of the archives of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution was granted access to these archives in October of 2000; however, we were never informed about that despite the fact that the trial was still ongoing at the time. But we will come back to this issue later during our submissions. Of course, this is not the time and the place to discuss this any further. The Defence asked that this be rejected under Rule 115. The Trial Chamber rejected our motion, for reasons that are justified by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that has evolved since. The appeals ground put forward by Mr. Cerkez. I would like to remind you first that the Cerkez Defence clearly defined all grounds for appeal in its filing of the 9th of March 2002. While our appeal is contained in the brief filed on the 9th of August 2001. This filing of the 9th of March 2002 is something that resulted from the request of the Pre-Appeals Judge, Mr. Hunt, who asked us to systemtise our filings in any way, which we did. My colleague Mr. Mikulicic and I will deal with five grounds for appeal. This is the total of all grounds we are putting forward. The first will be that the Trial Chamber erred in applying the Geneva Conventions of 1949, which refers to Article 2 of the Statute, specifically, to the issue of existence of the international armed conflict, and this will be dealt by my colleague Mr. Mikulicic. Then we will deal with individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3). The third ground of appeal is that the appellant did not have a fair trial because we believe that violations occurred of fundamental rights of the accused under Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute and Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure. Another ground of appeal is that a number of factual findings in the Trial Chamber judgement were made below the beyond reasonable doubt criterion. And our fifth ground of appeal is the issue of sentencing. Let me note that I will not take these grounds in sequence; in fact, my colleague Mr. Mikulicic will take up the first ground of appeal, the existence of an international armed conflict, first; and responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3) will be dealt in an abbreviated way, under the ground that has to do with sentencing; then my colleague Mr. Mikulicic will put forward our arguments concerning fair trial violation, Article 3, which is our third ground of appeal. And then I will take up our ground of appeal concerning the reasonable doubt criterion and sentencing. If the Appeals Chamber agrees with this, then I will give the floor to my colleague Mr. Mikulicic to take up the first ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is how in ancient Rome -- this is how in ancient Rome eminent judges addressed parties in proceedings. Give us facts and we will give you justice, because the court knows the law. This Latin sentence was one of the first that I learnt as a law student in my first year in learning the subject Roman law. My professor taught me that it is not the duty of parties to legal proceedings to teach the court how to apply the law, that it would be indecent and inappropriate, in fact, because it is the duty of the parties, instead, to familiarise the court with the factual situation. Now, addressing the Appeals Chamber, I have the embarrassing responsibility to approach the Court with our interpretation of the law, which we hope the Appeals Chamber will apply in the procedure to follow. I therefore ask for your understanding in advance if I fall into the trap of sounding excessively like a teacher. Following the report of Secretary-General of 3rd May 1993, the competencies of this Tribunal were defined, ratione materiae, so that the Tribunal is obliged to apply in its work the rules of international humanitarian law which, without a doubt, are an integral part of customary law. Allow me to quote part of the report of the Secretary-General, and in order to avoid possible interpretation mistakes, I will do that in English. So in Article 1(A) 34 of this report, it reads: [In English] "In the view of the Secretary-General, the application of the principle nullum crimen sine lege requires that the International Tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are, beyond any doubt, part of customary law." [Interpretation] In the next paragraph, and I will continue with the quotation, the report explains what kind of international customary law is meant, and I quote: [In English] "The part of the conventional international humanitarian law which has, beyond doubt, become part of the international customary law, is the law applicable in armed conflict, as embodied in the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949, for the protection of war victims, The Hague conventions number 4, respecting the laws and customs of war on land, and the regulations annexes thereto, of 18 October 1907. The convention of the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide, of 9 December 1948, and the charter of the international military tribunal of 8 August 1945." [Interpretation] So according to our understanding, these are the sources of international customary law and the purview of ratione materiae of this eminent Tribunal. Contrary to the principle of legality, nullum crimen sine lege, the Tribunal applies the law which, at the time of the commission of the crime which is the subject of these proceedings was, doubtlessly, covered by international customary law. In the opinion of numerous legal theoreticians, ad hoc courts like this Tribunal do not have the mandate to create precedents in international law because they are limited in their activity by the purpose of their establishment and the wishes of their founders. In this specific case, what is at issue is the interpretation of Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal, and in this connection, the sentence meted out by the Trial Chamber to our client, namely, in counts 15, 19, 30, 31, 33, and 35 of the judgement, in paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It follows from the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and especially judgement in Naletilic case, application of Article 2 of the Statute requires four prerequisites. First, the existence of an armed conflict; second, the existence of a nexus between the conflict and the crimes allegedly perpetrated; third, the armed conflict must be an international armed conflict; and fourth, the persons or property which are the subject of serious violations must be defined as protected persons. These conditions that we are familiar with are cumulative and not alternative. I believe the application of Article 2 of the Statute is not at issue in the context of international armed conflict. However, what the Defence finds controversial is the choice of criteria for defining the character of the armed conflict that occurred in Lasva Valley, tempore criminis, in the course of 1993. In fact, adequate application of the international customary law that was in force at the time. My learned friend Mr. Sayers said something about this, and I will follow up on his contribution, and I beg you to excuse any duplication. The Defence of Mr. Cerkez, contrary to the position of the Trial Chamber, which found that the armed conflict in question was an international one, believes that the armed conflict was in fact internal, and for that reason, the Trial Chamber should not have applied Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal and convicted our client under that provision. The issue of the character of the armed conflict is a legal issue, but it is also a factual one. The latter issue, especially if we speak about the territory of an internationally recognised state, Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it is not questionable that there were many local clashes among various participants, and by this I mean among various ethnicities and combinations of ethnicities, which again varied from region to region, almost from village to village. Contemporary historians described Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time as a country with a hundred wars. Each of these wars was special and particular. It is the position of the Cerkez Defence that when making the decision on the character of the conflict, specific circumstances that applied at the relevant time, in the relevant territory, have to be taken into account. Allow me to remind Your Honours of the various facts relevant to that conflict. It started as a conflict between the former Yugoslav People's Army and paramilitary formations, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. Between these three ethnicities - Serbs, Croats, and Muslims - in various areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, clashes occurred in various combinations. In some places, Serbs and Croats found themselves allied against Muslims. Elsewhere, Muslims and Serbs united against Croats. And in yet other places, to make the absurd more complete, Bosnian Muslims fought between themselves in the territory of the same internationally recognised state. I shall recall before this honourable Appeals Chamber Exhibit D34/2, which is a report compiled for the requirements of the Security Council five days after the incident, the war crime in Ahmici, and filed by the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations, Mr. Sacirbey. In this letter, he characterised the conflict in the Lasva Valley as a conflict where - I paraphrase - local moguls clashed over the distribution of food and arms. Therefore, as I already said, it is not possible to view the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a uniform administrative unit with the elements of statehood known by international law at the critical time. What applied to the territory of the Lasva Valley, for instance, was not true of events and circumstances, for instance, in Srebrenica or Sarajevo or Herzegovina. Therefore, we kindly ask of this Honourable Appeals Chamber to take into account all the peculiarities of the factual situation inherent in the territory covered by the indictment, and I am afraid that they will find little help in the precedents established by cases where the facts were completely different. However, it is the position of the Defence that the Trial Chamber erred in defining the character of this armed conflict, which started in mid-April 1993, in the area of Vitez and its environs between members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the HVO. The Defence agrees with the finding of the Trial Chamber - I refer you to paragraph 31 of the judgement - that the armed conflict in that area did not exist at all as protracted violence before the 3rd of -- before March -- before April 1993. It is not in issue that there was no presence of regular army units of the Republic of Croatia. That is the position accepted by the Trial Chamber. However, in paragraph 108 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found that in adjacent areas, such as Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, parts of units of Croatian army were observed, that is, the army of the Republic of Croatia. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, this circumstance is of crucial importance for judging the character of this armed conflict. This, explained by the fact that the very presence of the Croatian army in the neighbouring area was of strategic importance. Such findings in the judgement, and legal conclusions, are not in harmony with the actual situation, because, first of all, the units of Croatian army were located in an area which has no physical link to the Vitez area, which is where our client, Mr. Cerkez, was active. Moreover, the area of the Lasva Valley and the area of Gornji Vakuf and Prozor are separated by an impassable mountain chain, and this chain presents an insurmountable physical obstacle to any kind of communication. One can be assured of this just by looking at a map and by analysing the evidence presented in the trial. Second, the units of Croatian army, which in mid-1993 found themselves in Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, were there to assist the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in their defence against the attack by the units of the former JNA and Serbian paramilitary formations. This assistance and support of the Croatian army was based on the agreement reached between Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 21st of July, 1992, and therefore, I would like to bring to your attention Exhibit D98/1. The error made by Trial Chamber was evident also in erroneous definition of two elements which determine the character of an armed conflict. The first one is the so-called overall control test. I'm here referring to paragraph 111 of the judgement. And the second one pertains to the definition of protected persons under Article 4 of the fourth Geneva Convention, and here I am referring to paragraphs 147 to 160 of the judgement. Allow me to say a few words concerning the first issue. The so-called overall control test is a test used to determine the character of an armed conflict and was applied by this Tribunal for the first time in the appeals judgement in Tadic case on the 15th of July, 1999. Up until that time, as an undisputed element of international customary law, a different test was used, a so-called effective control test, from the well-known case, Nicaragua, dating back to 1986. Therefore, it is obvious that the test from the Tadic appeals judgement represents an application of law ex post facto, delicti commissi, therefore, after the crime committed, and application of the law in this manner is prejudicial to the defendant because the overall control test is a much broader test than the previous one that was used, based on which the Defence concludes that this represents a violation of the principle of legality. I think that it is well accepted that the principle of legality is an essential part of the international customary law. This principle has also been included in the so-called Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, and therefore, represents one of basic guarantees for a fair trial. Therefore, the position of the Defence is that, notwithstanding the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the application of a new definition pertaining to certain legal situations is completely unfounded, especially when in the previous period, those situations were defined in a completely different manner, and by this I'm referring to the time when the crimes were committed. Resorting to this kind of test, the Trial Chamber actually violated the rights of the accused. This was prejudicial to the accused. The Trial Chamber, de facto and de jure, introduced a new legal category and redefined an essential element under Article 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal and for the purposes of this article. Now I would like to turn to another issue, which is how the protected persons are defined, and especially how this was defined in the judgement that is now being reviewed on appeal. Therefore, the status of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the protected persons is actually conditio sine qua non in order to characterise a criminal act in accordance with Article 2 of the Statute. Protected persons are defined in Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, which state that in order to define this category, the persons affected must be persons who are of a different nationality than the persons under whose authority they are. In this particular case, it is clear that the victims in this case were Bosnian Muslims and that the accused were Bosnian Croats. It is also clear that both groups represent nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, in this particular case, in view of the Defence of Mr. Cerkez, we cannot discuss the definition of protected persons in such a way to ensure that this definition is in accordance with the formulation in Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions. Therefore, in paragraph 152 of the judgement, it is stated that the concept of protected persons should be teleologically interpreted. I have to admit that I was not entirely clear as to how would -- one manifestly clear provision could be interpreted in any way that is different from the formulation and the purpose of the formulation of that concept. The concept of protected persons defined in the 1949 Geneva Conventions has not been amended. Therefore, it is inappropriate that, depending on the needs of the trial, or this or that situation, a strictly defined concept be interpreted in a different way, be reformulated and made different from its original definition in the original text, especially if that text is a source of international humanitarian law, defining the subject matter jurisdiction of this Tribunal. Therefore, in the view of the Defence of Mr. Cerkez, the Trial Chamber took it upon themselves to redefine and reinterpret a clear formulation of Article 4, Geneva Conventions and thus create a new legal norm which, under 1, is not an element of accepted international customary law, which is referred to in the report of the general secretary from 1993. And second, this legal provision, which has redefined the Geneva Conventions, came into force in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal after the criminal acts were committed. And third, this is prejudicial to the accused. Therefore, the Defence concludes that it is inappropriate to apply teleological interpretation of formulation of Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, but that, instead of that, this article should be interpreted only in accordance with its original formulation. I would like to remind you that any analogy in such cases, in criminal law, is something every judge and every Trial Chamber should carefully avoid. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber, by applying properly international customary law, had to find that, in a given time and in a given place, there were no elements of international armed conflict and that, therefore, substantive law could not be applied in accordance with Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal. I would like to add several elements to this argument. Article 4(2) of the fourth Geneva Convention from 1949 goes on to say that nationals of a party to the war should not be considered as protected persons as long as the state whose nationals they are continues to have normal diplomatic relations with the state under whose authority these persons are. If we apply this to the facts of this case, then we come to the following conclusion: That Bosnian Muslims, as nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were in the hands or were victims who were under the authority of Bosnian Croats, who are also nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even if we suppose that Bosnian Croats were agents of the Republic of Croatia, which this Defence vigorously disputes, even under those circumstances, if we apply the Geneva Conventions, Article 4(2), these persons cannot be characterised as protected persons. Why is this so? Because from the moment when the Republic of Croatia, as the first UN member state, recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state, so from that day until nowadays, not for a moment, not in any way, were the diplomatic relations between these two countries disrupted. On the contrary; these diplomatic relations exist at the level of embassies. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had its own military mission throughout the conflict, both in Zagreb and in Split. The entire logistics, humanitarian aid, assistance given to the wounded and to the refugees, went through the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And even those items which were prohibited by the resolution of the Security Council went through. This prohibition pertained to weapons. All of the weapons flowed into Bosnia and Herzegovina, exclusively through the territory and by using transportation means of the Republic of Croatia. Now I would like to ask you, Your Honours: What state which intervenes as an aggressor in another state would provide to their enemies weapons, food, take care of the other state's wounded and the refugees in their own territory? Therefore, it is absurd to come to this conclusion. I would like to point out to another provision of the Geneva Conventions, which is Article 2(1) of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, which sets forth that 2 belligerent parties do not have to declare war to each other in order for the international conflict to exist, but at least one of the parties to the conflict, at least one of the participants, has to be aware that there is an armed conflict. No matter how hard you try, nowhere will you find an official statement or a declaration or anything similar that would point to this suggestion that Bosnia and Herzegovina at any time during the conflict in the Lasva Valley objected or qualified the conflict as an international armed one. Throughout the time summit conferences continued, numerous agreements were reached, and I will recall here the joint declaration by Tudjman and Izetbegovic from the 14th of September, 1993 -- 1992, which said that the conflicts between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO were of local proportions. In this connection, I would like to turn to one more issue. It is indubitable that armed conflicts did occur throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is indubitable that some of them were international and others were internal. However, in this specific instance, there is really no legal ground or factual evidence to support the finding on the existence of an international armed conflict. If the eminent Judges have any questions on this subject, I am ready to respond, before I move to the following ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Pocar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, I would like to be clear about your position on some arguments you made here. In particular, as concerns the test to be applied. If I got correctly what you said, you challenged the legitimacy of the overall control test that was applied in Tadic and in other cases by this Appeals Chamber, on the basis that it is looser than the effective control test that was applied by the International Court of Justice in Nicaragua a few years earlier. Am I correct that your argument implies that first the Nicaragua test adopted by the ICJ was correct, and second, that the assessment of the ICJ, as far as customary international law is shaped, is final, irrespective of the specific situation put before the court, and does not allow for a different assessment of customary international law by anybody else? Is that your opinion, your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Pocar, I would like to answer your question in two ways. First, it is the view of the Defence that the so-called overall control test is in fact inaugurated -- was in fact inaugurated after the commission of the relevant crimes. Accordingly, that test was not part of the international customary law in 1993. Rather, it became, if it did, part of that law after 1993, which presents us with a problem: Will the Chamber apply a de facto legal norm adopted after the perpetration of the crime or not? In my view, such a legal norm could be applied only if it is more favourable to the accused. If that legal norm, in the view of the Defence, is more detrimental to the accused, more prejudicial, then it cannot be applied, and we believe it indeed to be less favourable because the test of the effective control from the Nicaragua case is more rigorous and requires that more precise and stricter elements be met than is true of the Tadic case, the overall control test. Let me conclude. The Cerkez Defence believes that, with the application of this test inaugurated ex post facto delicto delicti commissi the Trial Chamber applied a less favourable legal norm from the point of view of the accused, and did so inappropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. But in order to be clear: Your point is that the test was inaugurated after the commission of the crime because the assessment was made after the commission of the crime does not allow for the possibility that the -- a Chamber in 2000 may assess the law in 1992 or in 1991, customary on that occasion, unless, as I said earlier, you consider that the test is indicated by the ICJ had to be considered final unless replaced by another test. So at the end, you seem to come to say that the test indicated by the ICJ had to be considered final for everybody until the moment, maybe, in which a new assessment is made by another body. But until that new assessment is thus made, in between, that law would apply in any case. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is precisely the position of the Defence team of Mr. Cerkez. As long as the old norm is not replaced by a new one, it remains in force. The new norm starts to apply when it enters into force, and applies to all the crimes committed after its entry into force. That is the position of our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't want to prolong too much this debate, but don't you think that in doing so, you give the ICJ the power to codify international law, to decide what international law is, in general terms, and this task has not been attributed to the ICJ, not even by the charter of the United Nations. It just says the ICJ is a judicial organ that has to assess customary international law for the purpose of the case, but it in any case cannot codify the law as such. I mean, other bodies within the UN system have the task to codify international law, as the case may be. What would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I agree with you completely, Your Honour, and I can only say that the same argument which you just put forward applies to this International Tribunal as well, with one difference, namely, that this Tribunal was established with strictly defined competencies and that it is an ad hoc Tribunal, and it is a question, in legal theory, whether an ad hoc tribunal may create precedents at all which would affect international law as such. And I believe the International Criminal Court of Justice codifies the criminal law and the international customary law in a way; however, the rules that apply to the ICJ cannot apply to this Tribunal, for two reasons, namely, that this Tribunal was established after the commission of the acts and because it is an ad hoc Tribunal with a strictly limited time frame. I suppose that we lawyers can discuss this for a long time to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Your position is quite clear to me now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will allow me, Your Honours, to move on to our grounds for appeal from paragraph 3, very briefly, I'm afraid, to present the arguments of our Defence team that our client was deprived of a fair trial because his fundamental rights granted by Article 20 and 20.1 of the Statute and Rule 89 were violated. What is at issue here? The issue is that the Defence detected prima facie at least eight infractions that it would qualify as violations of the right to a fair trial. Having said that, the Defence does not claim that each of the violations is of such proportions and such a nature that it would io ipso, lead to an invalidation of the findings of the Trial Chamber. But I would like to point to certain practice in regular criminal courts. Speaking of qualifications of physical injuries, legal theoreticians have already made a distinction between lighter and more serious injuries, bodily injuries. However, there is one more category, namely, a great number of lighter bodily injuries taken together qualify as a serious bodily injury, serious physical injury, although each one taken apart is not serious. However, combined in a certain number, they qualify as a serious injury. Something similar was mentioned in the procedure that preceded this trial, this appeal. Namely, our client was prevented from testifying on his behalf. During its case, the Prosecution continuously disclosed new evidence, and my colleague Mr. Sayers spoke of this at great length, and very eloquently. The Defence, under the decision of the Trial Chamber, was not given appropriate facilities to prepare its closing argument and its final brief. Furthermore, despite two orders to disclose documentation issued to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and despite the promises made by the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who said explicitly that they are in possession of documentation that could be useful in the proceedings, these documents were not made available until the end of the trial. At the end of the trial, the Defence was prepared to put the accused on the stand and let him present to the Trial Chamber his version of the events. We are convinced that he is the right person to do this because no one knows better than he what exactly happened and how. The Defence thought that his testimony would be extremely valuable in shedding light on certain aspects and circumstances that remained insufficiently clear. His testimony was envisaged for a Monday, namely, the 16th of October, 2000, at 9.00. The Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to provide the Defence, in a timely manner, with the material on the basis of which they intend to cross-examine our client. What happened? This material was not made available to the Defence before Friday, the 13th, which must be an unfortunate date. That is precisely the weekend before our client's testimony was to take place. At 10.00 p.m., the Defence received a pile of documents, 40 centimetres thick, which it was supposed to review before Monday. We were, of course, physically unable to go through these documents in time and prepare, and even less were we able to contact our client in the Detention Unit to go through the documents together with him and possibly hear his comments. First of all, during the weekend, the lawyers are not entitled to visit their clients in the Detention Unit; and second, this time would have been insufficient anyway. Therefore, we were forced to advise our client to renounce this opportunity to testify, simply because we did not know what we would face further on in the proceedings. We believe that, as a result of the acts of the Prosecution, which the Trial Chamber did not sanction in any way and did not revise them, the Defence was greatly prejudiced by the very fact that our client was prevented from testifying. Similarly, the things unfolded when it came to the preparation of our final brief and the closing arguments. Your Honours, this case is one of the most complex cases ever to be held before the international criminal court until that time. You heard how many trial days were spent here. You also heard how many witnesses testified here, how many exhibits were admitted. So you could conclude that it was a very complex case. My colleague Mr. Kovacic told you that the Cerkez case originally was part of a case that was later split into four separate cases. When the Defence appealed to the Trial Chamber to allow us, in this very complex case, where there was a continuous flow of new material, to allow us extra time to prepare our final brief and closing arguments, the Trial Chamber denied our request. We asked for the same amount of time that was given to other Defence teams in other Lasva Valley cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
