In Aleksovski they received three weeks, and five weeks in Kupreskic case. All of these cases are Lasva Valley cases, and they're all very similar. However, we were denied our request, and we received only three working days. And this came after 240-something days of trial, 28.000 pages of transcript and so on. As a result, we believe that our client was denied equality of arms. We believe that this was prejudicial to our client, and we would like to bring to your attention a quote from the Aleksovski appeals judgement wherein paragraph 24 it says: [In English] "A reasonable opportunity to present his case." [Interpretation] Similarly, I would also like to bring to your attention the opinion of Judge Hunt in the trial judgement in Aleksovski case where he said: [In English] "I also agree with the judgement, that the Trial Chamber is not bound by the decision of another Trial Chamber, although I believe that it should have respect for that decision and consider carefully whether it is appropriate to depart from it." [Interpretation] In our case, in our view, the Trial Chamber denied us the practice that was customary here at this Tribunal where the Defence is given additional time to prepare closing arguments and final briefs, especially in a case like this one where we were unable to do so during the trial for the -- because we were continuously receiving new material, new exhibits, and that especially intensified in the last two months of this trial. I would like to close my arguments by stating that our Defence team adheres to the grounds of appeal as stated in our appellant's brief and further elaborated in our response to the Prosecution's brief. Should you have any questions, I am available to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding your question on the transcript, I just discovered that my computer failed, and I cannot go through the pages of the transcripts, but I do know the date. It was on 17 October 2000, the beginning of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Literally on the beginning, because we started that morning with that discussion. [Interpretation] I would like to touch upon two or three procedural errors and follow up on what my colleague Mr. Mikulicic said. We believe that taken as a whole, these errors significantly -- significantly violated the right of our client to have a fair trial. I will also discuss the testimony of Witness AT, which was elaborated also by the Defence of Mr. Kordic, and here I would like to speak only about the part of this witness's testimony which we refer to as hearsay evidence, and in this regard I would like to refer you to paragraph 8, page 43 of our brief, as well as paragraphs 11 to 13, pages 44 to 45. We have similar objections with respect to Witness Nihad Rebihic. This is mentioned in paragraph 44(G) on page 101 of our appeals brief. The judgement states that solely on the basis of the testimony of Witness AT, the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that our client, Mr. Cerkez, was present at the military meeting held in Blaskic's offices on the 15th of April, 1993, in late afternoon towards the evening, and at that meeting a plan of attack on the Bosnian Muslims was drafted. The attack was to take place on the following day. This is mentioned in paragraphs 630 and 631 of the judgement, the last sentence of paragraph 631 pertains to Mr. Cerkez. This is an essential finding of the Trial Chamber which later on leads the Trial Chamber to conclude that Cerkez and the soldiers who were subordinated to him perpetrated crimes in Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that paragraph 630 of the trial judgement, I will read it out in English: [In English] "Thus, in deciding whether to accept -- whether to accept the evidence of Witness AT, the Trial Chamber must determine to what extent his evidence is confirmed by other evidence. In fact, there is no direct evidence supporting his account of the meeting. However, there is circumstantial evidence which does so." [Interpretation] Following this finding, the judgement gives several instances of circumstantial evidence which, in Trial Chamber's view, corroborate the testimony of Witness AT. However, following that, the judgement reads as follows: [In English] "These matters, by themselves, would not be sufficient to lead the Trial Chamber to accept the witness evidence." [Interpretation] After that, the judgement goes on to say and to assess coherence and credibility of the witness and concludes as follows: [In English] "Although he could not bring himself to tell the full truth of his own involvement in the attack and the Trial Chamber finds that he was mistaken in his evidence about the use of the mosque for defence purposes, which is not supported by the evidence of other witnesses, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that he did tell the truth about the preparations for the Ahmici attack, including the meetings at Hotel Vitez and the subsequent briefings." [Interpretation] Based on this finding that I just read out in paragraph 630, in the following paragraph, 631, they conclude as follows: [In English] "The Chamber is also satisfied that Mario Cerkez, as a commander of the Viteska Brigade, was present at the military meeting which followed the politicians' meeting." [Interpretation] These findings, in our view, have three significant flaws which clearly show that this finding of the Trial Chamber, namely that Cerkez was present at the meeting, does not meet the required standard, which is beyond reasonable doubt. And in support of this, I state as follows: First of all, Witness AT did not say anything about the matters discussed at that military meeting. The witness doesn't know what was agreed upon at that meeting. The witness was not present at the meeting. He learned about the fact that the meeting would be held from his Commander Pasko Ljubicic. Therefore, in that respect, his testimony is a typical example of hearsay. Second, as regards the inference that Cerkez was present at the meeting, there are -- there is direct documentary evidence showing that Cerkez was not present at the meeting. Therefore, there is something that fully contradicts the hearsay evidence of Witness AT, and this can be found in Exhibit 610.1. Regardless of the views taken by other parties in this trial, including both the Prosecutor and Mr. Kordic, the Prosecutor, in their final brief, expressed some doubts concerning that document. They were of the opinion that that document should be taken into account only selectively. [In English] I would kindly ask the usher to assist me. [Interpretation] So some parts of that document do have a certain value. As regards the meeting, the document that I just mentioned, 610, does refer to the meeting. In English that's on page 58. [In English] This is page -- little bit up so the number of the page could be seen. No, no. The bottom of the page. This is page 68 in English translation, and it is here clearly recorded who was present at that military meeting. Cerkez was not among them. There is no Viteska Brigade commander. [Interpretation] I wish to remind the Honourable Judges at this point of one fact: The judgement deals with this in detail, and you have heard a lot about this meeting through our submissions. To avoid any misunderstanding, it seems quite indisputable that first three meetings were held at the hotel, followed by two meetings at the Bungalow in Nadioci. The first meeting, and we still to this day don't know whether it was held or not, was a meeting of political leaders, and then later, towards the evening, a military meeting followed. And I suppose that the Trial Chamber carefully chose the adjective "military." After that evening meeting, according to Witness AT, a meeting was held in the TV room of the hotel attended exclusively, according to his testimony, by members of the military police, and that is evidently so because there is no evidence to the contrary. And later on, two more meetings were held at the Bungalow in Nadioci attended by only members of the military police, two briefings. The claim was that Cerkez attended only one meeting, namely the second one, which was a meeting of military commanders in the office of Colonel Blaskic. However, the duty officer's log, Exhibit 610.1, constitutes direct evidence contrary to that assertion that Cerkez attended that meeting. And essentially, my argument is this: We have two conflicting pieces of evidence. One is hearsay evidence of Witness AT, who says that Cerkez was present at the meeting. The second one is a document from which it transpires that Cerkez did not attend. Ergo, if a criminal plan was made at that meeting such as a plan that involved the killing of civilians, Cerkez could not have known about it. Furthermore, and this fact is very important, the same witness, AT, later on in his testimony, that is transcript page 27668, explicitly says that the first time he explicitly heard about killing orders was at the Bungalow in Nadioci. What is the implication of this, the statement that this was the first time? The implication is that it was not mentioned at the military meeting which, by the way, my client did not attend. But even if he had attended, and that is my second argument, he still would not have learned of any criminal plan because no criminal plan was discussed there. And in conclusion of this part, the Chamber thus had two possible conclusions open to it, two conflicting conclusions. Either he was there or he wasn't. And according to the principle of in dubio pro reo, the Trial Chamber should have, without a doubt, found in favour of my client, namely that he did not attend. That is the only conclusion that could have been arrived at according to the in dubio pro reo principle. In order to avoid any loose ends, and we have clearly put this on the table before, Cerkez does not deny that he did meet with Blaskic on the 15th, the evening of the 15th at the hotel, but it was a bilateral meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My apologies, but apparently there are two different copies we have available, one from the Registry and the one you put on the ELMO. It's not totally the same document, and if I may ask the usher, please, to show the top of this page. Apparently only some additions made in handwriting on the document which forms part of the record and is in the position of the Registry. However, it doesn't change anything as to the content. I only wanted to refer to the B/C/S version where it reads apparently at 950 that due to this book Mr. Cerkez was present. Please correct me if I'm wrong. Unfortunately, these pages are not numbered in B/C/S. It's the same day, 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about to start that sentence when you asked the question. The Defence never denied that Cerkez did not meet with his commander, Blaskic; but it was a bilateral meeting. By all appearances, and we haven't been able to establish this for certain, this meeting was after the one just mentioned. Why? There is clear evidence in the case, and I will refer you to it in a moment, there is clear evidence that on the 15th of April, 1993, in the afternoon, Cerkez was scheduled to attend a wedding ceremony at church. Cerkez had been married before, but he wanted to marry in church again because that was the wish of his wife, and that was scheduled for the 15th of April, 1993, at 6.30 p.m. That is Exhibit D94/2, and direct testimony was provided on this by witness Stipo Ceko transcript page 23439, and another witness priest Drago Pranjes on transcript page 26127, as well as Witness C1 in the Kupreskic case, page 11136. Thus Cerkez did go to the wedding, and I can provide the document if you wish me to do so, but let us not waste more time. When they were departing from the house, and I'm referring to testimony of Witness Ceko, and getting into the cars, a telephone call came, and Cerkez was invited to see Blaskic, but that happened after this meeting. We don't dispute either that Cerkez received a verbal order there concerning his mission for the next day, the 16th of April. And this verbal order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please be more concrete on the hours? We have in this logbook a number of entries where your client is mentioned. For example, 12.50 hours, Colonel Blaskic called Mario Cerkez, gave instructions. And some other entries before, since -- when was the first one. At 9.50, for example. So it can't be only once. If the logbook is correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not only for that day but also for the other days, it is obvious from the logbook that Cerkez had contacts with his commander, which was only natural. On that day, if I'm not mistaken, he had some contacts in the morning and one contact in the early evening. We are simply unable to say at what time exactly, but it was certainly after 5.30 p.m. Probably around 6.00 p.m. Cerkez wanted to testify about this, among other things, but he was unable to. It transpires from Exhibit D94/2 that the wedding was scheduled Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for 6.30 p.m. We assume that they departed from home around 30 minutes before. So he must have received this telephone call before 6.00. And if we take into account the time it took him to get to the Vitez Hotel by car, we suppose he could not be there before 6.30 under any circumstance. Whether it was 6.30 or 7.00 p.m., it was early evening. And according to the information we have about this meeting we see referred to in 610.1, which took place at 5.30, in fact started at 5.30, then Cerkez could only have arrive one hour late at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please allow a question by Judge Weinberg de Roca. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: I don't know if it's the translation, but perhaps you could be a bit more precise, because in the English we have a lot of -- you assume the time, it could have been at that time, or it could have been at that other time, but your client is here. He wanted to testify. You can consult with him. So perhaps we could have some precision. It was the day you explained of his wedding, so I'm sure he must remember at what time he was married, what time he left headquarters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is precisely the point. When we discussed this the first time while we were preparing our Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- even then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... He wants to say that Mr. Kovacic can't testify on behalf of his client today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That is the objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only a problem of testifying here today. I'm afraid that we may appear as wanting a trial de novo. We are perfectly aware that we are not supposed to retry the case, and I am going into this detail now only on the basis of the claim that the finding of the Trial Chamber does not meet the beyond a reasonable doubt criteria. And in order to show that I have to point to some evidence that supports my claim. And to make matters worse, it is our position, as my colleague indicated earlier, the problem is precisely that our client was unable to testify, and this assertion was not corroborated by any other evidence. I must ask the Appeals Chamber to take into account that we introduced this exhibit, D94/2, during trial and brought witnesses who testified that this wedding was indeed scheduled for the 15th of April, 1993, for 6.30 p.m., and from this evidence, namely the testimony of Stipo Ceko and the affidavit of Ruza Ceko accompanying this testimony, it clearly transpires that they were leaving their houses, which were next to each other, getting into their cars and driving to the church for the wedding. The witness testifies that at precisely at that moment, the telephone call came. Cerkez had to go back to his house and to leave. So the wedding did not take place. And if we are aware of how long it took to get from one point to another, we can reasonably assume that it took 20 minutes to get to the church. We can also assume that it took him about ten minutes to change into his military uniform and drive there. And even if he was very quick about it, he could not have been at the hotel before 6.30. He could only have been there later. But I'm not testifying about this. I am only explaining the basis for my argument. My argument is that Cerkez did not attend the meeting, and the finding of the Trial Chamber is based solely on the hearsay testimony of Witness AT, which is unreliable and thin and contradicted by two pieces of direct evidence, Exhibit Z610.1, and Exhibit D94/2, supported by the testimony of two witnesses. I wish to tell this Appeals Chamber very clearly that Cerkez did meet with Blaskic at the hotel alone. He received verbal orders at that meeting, verbal orders that were typed up during the night and given to him in writing later. That is Exhibit D60/2, and Cerkez did precisely as he was instructed to in this order. Later on I will come back to the part pertaining to the implementation of that order, and now I would like to further discuss the errors which resulted in fair trial violations. The next issue that I would like to touch upon here is that we believe that there is a problem with the authenticity of Exhibit Z692/3, namely this exhibit was particularly referred to in the judgement in paragraph 689(c). We mention this document in our appeals brief, in paragraph 24, 24(c), 25, and, as I said, in the judgement it's mentioned in paragraph 689(c), and relied on in findings in paragraph 691. It is also mentioned in one other place in the judgement, 689(a), where the Trial Chamber mentions Exhibit Z692.2, which was never admitted into evidence. Let me explain this: Paragraph 691 of the judgement states that, I'm quoting: [In English] "The Trial Chamber concludes that these documents clearly establish that the Viteska Brigade was in the thick of the fighting and that Mario Cerkez was in command of the brigade. In particular, the brigade took part in operations in Vitez, Veceriska, and Ahmici during 16 April 1993 in breaks, but only later in the day and not during the initial assault on Ahmici." [Interpretation] Therefore, this finding of the Trial Chamber is both favourable and not favourable for Cerkez. On one hand, it is unfavourable because based on this and some other documents, the Trial Chamber concluded that Cerkez was involved in the Vitez operation as well as in Veceriska, and at the same time, the Trial Chamber found that Cerkez was not present in Ahmici, which is favourable for our client, at least that he wasn't present there in the initial stage when these crimes were committed. These findings of the Trial Chamber were based on evidence which was carefully analysed in paragraph 689 A through F. Under A this paragraph first lists exhibit 692.2 which was never admitted into evidence. The Prosecution agreed with this in their response, which can be found in their response, paragraph 10.19 and 10.20. Therefore, if one analyses paragraph 689 of the judgement, one can see that there are several facts analysed here which are used to base the findings upon. The first document mentioned in this analysis was never introduced into evidence. Therefore, it cannot be used to base a finding upon it, and the Prosecution agrees with this. The next document in that analysis mentioned in paragraph 689(c) of the judgement is something that Defence deems to be a forgery. There were 4.665 exhibits admitted into evidence in this trial. In addition to that there were several thousand other documents which were not admitted, all of these documents were copies, and we never ever challenged the authenticity of any of the copies. The only document whose authenticity was challenged by us was precisely this exhibit mentioned in paragraph 6923 and there are many reasons to challenge the authenticity of this document. I don't need to go into them now. It is our position that copies can be used as evidence in trial but only as long as one of the parties does not challenge the authenticity of a copy. As soon as one party challenges the authenticity of the document, the other party must either produce an original or produce other evidence to authenticate the challenged document. We believe this to be a general rule to be applied in criminal trials. This is true for national courts, and I don't think that it needs to be further elaborated. This document appeared without Defence ever seeing it before, so this document appeared on the 5th of October, 2000, when Witness Anto Bertovic gave evidence, and the Prosecution, in cross-examination, presented this document. On page 25954 of the transcript, this is what Bertovic said about this document: "Well, I personally did not see this document before. This command or this type of command never reached me, and perhaps I can think of an explanation. It may be because the Vitez Brigade was not capable at all especially my battalion of anything like this. I personally never received this document and I do not know that the Vitez Brigade received it either. I know nothing about it all." Then a little bit later on 26003 and 25997, the same witness said -- the same witness was also talking about that document. [Interpretation] This document was not shown to the Defence prior to that day, and this is why the Defence was denied an opportunity to challenge the document. This is referred to in pages 55 to 58 of our appellant's brief. And perhaps I should add another matter, which is that the same document was used in cross-examination of another witness by Prosecution, Witness Zuljevic on the 8th of December 2000 on page 28196 of the transcript. This witness reacted in a similar way and I will read to you what the witness said. [In English] "This, this is an outrage. This doesn't look like Colonel Blaskic. He was aware of the fact that we did not have any manpower. Gentlemen, I have been saying consistently, and I'm sure that in Donja Veceriska, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, and Vrhovine in particular at that time on the 16 of April, there were never activities on the part of the Viteska Brigade. And now what this order refers to I really cannot understand, and I cannot explain it for sure." [Interpretation] Let me show you this document, 692.3. We will put it on ELMO. Based on this document, Cerkez was ordered, and this document is dated 16th of April, 1993, at 10.35 hours, so this document orders Cerkez to go to Donja Veceriska, Sivrino Selo, and Vrhovine. So Sivrino Selo and Vrhovine, two out of four places mentioned in the document were never once mentioned throughout the war as places where there was any conflict. It was established that Cerkez was not present in Donja Veceriska on that morning, and at any rate, this does not implicate Cerkez because the crime in Ahmici was over by 10.35. One thing that is important for Cerkez is that this order mentions Donja Veceriska. On the other hand, there were many exhibits which corroborate the Defence case of Cerkez, one of them being that Cerkez and his unit were never present in Donja Veceriska, and even had they been there, which is something that Defence denies, even had they been there, there were no crimes committed there. There was just a legal military operation implemented there. There were no crimes against civilians in that place. So these are the issues that I qualify as violations of fair trial guarantees. In addition to that, in my view these two documents demonstrate that one of important findings concerning Cerkez's involvement in certain locations do not meet beyond the reasonable doubt standard, because careful analysis shows that the findings of the Trial Chamber are not in accordance with evidence presented. In conclusion of our third ground of appeal pertaining to fair trial guarantees, I would like to go back to something that my colleague has mentioned in the beginning. We can agree that none of the errors that my colleague mentioned and that I have mentioned are on their own so grave that they would justify the reversal of judgement. We agree with that claim. However, we submit that a more realistic approach should be applied here; namely, the Chamber must realise that a series of such errors, we have pointed only the main ones here and the rest are in our appellant's brief, therefore that a series of such errors definitely -- definitely affected the right of our client to a fair trial. Therefore, we propose that Cerkez be acquitted of all counts, because taken together, all of these errors have violated his statutory guarantees to fair trial to that extent that this can only be cured by invalidation of trial judgement. I don't know how much time we have left; however, I hope that I will be able to conclude within the next ground of appeal within the 30 minutes. If you have any questions, Your Honours, I am ready for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You still have 30 minutes, until 5.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] If there are no questions, I would then like to move on to the next ground of appeal which in our chronology is the second ground. To save time, I will not go into great detail. This ground of appeal has to do with criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3). We discussed this in our appellant's brief on pages 23 to 33 and in our reply to Prosecution's response on pages 10 to 13. Later on when I speak about the sentencing, I will also touch upon this -- these articles, 7(1) and 7(3), because I think that it would be more logical to do it at that time. Therefore, I would like to move on to the fourth ground of appeal, which deals with the fact that several factual findings of the Trial Chamber were also flawed and not in accordance with the standard beyond reasonable doubt. In our brief, we explain in detail how the Defence believes that the erroneous findings of the Trial Chamber, which established our -- that our client was guilty of crimes committed in Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska locations. These findings can be found in paragraph 601, 610 to 612, 619, 621, 630, as we have already mentioned, 631, last sentence of that paragraph as we have also already mentioned; and then paragraph 642, 691, 703, 809, 831, 836, 842, and 843. In our brief, we also mention this in paragraphs 1 to 4 in the introductory segment and then later on throughout the brief. As for the counts, we refer here to counts 2, 5, and 6, 14, 15, 17, 19, 41 to 44, 42. So this is what it mostly deals with. Your Honours, I don't think there is a need to explain in great detail that if the factual findings are erroneous, and they are erroneous because they don't meet the required standard, which is beyond reasonable doubt, then such erroneous factual findings are obviously flawed because inappropriate substantive law was applied to them, and here we are referring to Article 25.1(B) of the Statute. Violations of substantive law necessarily result in miscarriage of justice, and in that respect, all I wish to say is that if the relevant findings of the Trial Chamber were not made in accordance with the required standard, namely beyond reasonable doubt, then this necessarily leads to erroneous factual findings and other flaws in application of substantive law. At this point, I would like to indicate certain instances. We made at least eight or nine such references in our appellant's brief, and I will deal only with the most important ones, noting that we of course adhere to all of them as substantiated in our appellant's brief. First of all, we believe that there is insufficient evidence judged by the beyond reasonable doubt standard to conclude that the appellant was aware of the alleged plan made by the HVO on the 16th of April. We refer to paragraphs 610, 611, 612, 613, and 631 of the judgement. In these findings of the judgement, we read that Cerkez allegedly knew of the so-called criminal plan of the HVO for the 16th of April, 1993. The -- that is the first basis for the Trial Chamber's conclusion about Cerkez's mens rea. He must have known, according to the Trial Chamber, of this plan in order to be liable for the acts committed. That has to do with count 2, persecution; count 5, 6 -- 5 and 6, assault on civilian and civilian institutions, destruction not justified by military necessity, murder, et cetera. The judgement says that at the alleged meeting of the 15th of April in Blaskic's headquarters, a criminal plan was devised. The conclusion about the existence of that criminal plan is based on the testimony of Witness AT, as I mentioned earlier. We attack this conclusion because this is hearsay evidence and because there is documentary evidence to the contrary showing that Cerkez could not have attended the meeting where the alleged criminal plan was designed, and furthermore, later on in his testimony, Witness AT, on transcript page 27668, testified that the first time he heard about the alleged criminal plan was at the Bungalow. The meeting that Cerkez, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. according to the Trial Chamber, attended could only have discussed legitimate military plan, and this is corroborated by evidence we have on the events of the following day. I shall not elaborate any further on that meeting. I believe I have covered all the important points. More detail can be found in our appellant's brief. I only wish to emphasise that this plan, in fact the conclusions of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 630 and 631 formed the basis for the later establishment of Cerkez's liability for his alleged participation in acts committed in Donja Veceriska and Stari Vitez. Although there is abundant evidence on the record that Cerkez took part in preparing legitimate military action, defensive military action, and the judgement refers to that evidence, it is not explained anywhere in the judgement why the Defence case that this was defence activity was rejected. This is another reason why the Defence believes that the finding was made below the reasonable doubt standard. Another finding of that kind can be found in paragraph 691, 689, and 690. That is the finding that the Viteska Brigade was in the thick of the fighting and was, therefore, involved in the fighting in the Lasva Valley on the 16th of April. In paragraph 691, the Trial Chamber concludes that these documents clearly establish that: [In English] "...Mario Cerkez was in command of the brigade. In particular the brigade took part in operations in Vitez, Veceriska, and Ahmici during 16 April, but only later in the day and not during the initial assault on Ahmici." [Interpretation] I referred earlier to the relevant evidence that finding was made in paragraph 689(a) to (f), and I will not repeat it here. One the first elements analysed and used to lay the foundation for the judgement was documentary evidence which was not admitted into evidence or represented a forgery. In paragraph 601, the Trial Chamber rejects the claim of the Defence concerning the low level of organisation and readiness of the Viteska Brigade on the eve of the events. We respond to that in paragraphs 26 to 29 on pages 58 to 69 of our appellant's brief. In this paragraph it says: [In English] "The Trial Chamber, having considered the evidence, is satisfied that this picture of organisation and confusion presented by the Defence is not correct and that the brigade was sufficiently well organised and established to carry out the tasks allotted to it on 16 April 1993." [Interpretation] Cerkez, however, points out that the unit under his command was insufficiently organised, and it's sufficiently strong to perform the relevant tasks on several locations at the same time. Namely, on the 15th of April, Blaskic issued four military orders, all four of them having been entered into evidence, Exhibit D60/2, D343/1-6, D343/1-7, and D343/1-8. In these documents, these four orders issued by Blaskic that were entered into evidence, Cerkez received the included a definition of his zone of operation for the following day. His assignment was to take position in the -- in the area of defence, to block the villages and prevent entry and exit in these villages. The location is precisely described in the order which says that an attack of the enemy is expected from the direction of Kruscica towards the centre of the town and from Vranjska to the centre of the town. This order was presented several time during trial to a number of soldiers. If you allow for a moment my colleagues from the Prosecution promised to share with us a map that I would like to put on the screen showing the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is a good occasion to put two questions to you. The map now is already admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And second, please allow me this question having been not in the area at all. We found throughout the judgement the mentioning of Vitez and Stari Vitez. Am I correct in assuming that Stari Vitez is part or forms part of Vitez? It's the old town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. That is one and the same town, and it is difficult to discern the difference at first even if the local residents are able to show you that one part of the town is called Stari Vitez, whereas the other one is called Kolonija. That is one and the same town, and if you look at the map on the video evidence screen, the map doesn't show any difference either, but Stari Vitez would be the north-west section in the form of the triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your submission that it is incorrect to charge your client twice for crimes committed in Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, especially because this is an issue of semantics. That is one, as you pointed out. Vitez and Stari Vitez are one and the same location. However, there is another matter. It is absurd to talk of any HVO attacks on the part of the town, conditionally speaking, on the part of Vitez, excluding the other part of the town. There was no one to attack there, because the part of the town called Vitez was a base for the HVO from the beginning, unlike the other part, Stari Vitez. That was the headquarters of Blaskic, the headquarters of Cerkez. They could not have attacked themselves. It is absurd to talk of any attacks on Vitez. It is another matter that some people were arrested in the Vitez part of town, but my client was not charged with these arrests, and there is evidence that it was done by the civilian police, not the military police. My client was charged only with detention, not arrests. So when we speak of locations, we believe, actually, there are two locations critical for my client. One of them is Donja Veceriska, which is found a little to the left from Vitez on this map, along this horizontal line, Donja Veceriska. And the second one -- yes, we can speak of Stari Vitez only inasmuch as it was a part of town which held the TO headquarters of the BH army, and as soon as the conflict broke out between the two parties, the line was drawn there and the town was divided. With your leave, and I believe we could conclude this part with this, I would like to show the evidence we discussed, the first one being D60/2. [In English] If you would please turn the page on the English text. [Interpretation] That order defines the zone of responsibility, the military area of responsibility of my client in such a way that between the centre of town, the town of Vitez on one hand and Kruscica and Vranjska on the other hand. On the map these villages are found to the south of the town. The second order, 343/1, was issued to the civilian police, and their assignment and zone of possibility were clearly defined as being in the centre of town, because the order mentions some key features and key buildings. Thus according to this military order issued by Blaskic, this unit is in the centre of town with a task of protecting key buildings. The third order was issued by Blaskic. All of them were issued on the 16th of April early in the morning. That third order was issued to the commander of the Vitezovi battalion, one of the greatest military forces of the HVO at the time, and their assignment was defined on the axis of the firehouse to the bus station to the HVO headquarters, which means towards the part of town called Stari Vitez. The evidence is absolutely clear about this. There is no doubt that it concerns the firehouse and the bus station which are found in this part of town. And the fourth order -- now we are seeing the third one, and it is followed by another one addressed to the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, Ljubicic, who was ordered to occupy the road from Ahmici to Nadioci. That is the north-east area below the town. What exactly happened there is not something I'm going to discuss at this point, but if we look at these four orders combined, and if we look at a map of Vitez, it is indubitable that the order assigns Cerkez to be on the right side towards Kruscica and Vranjska. The Vitezovi have positions to the west, and the military police are assigned to be on the axis towards Ahmici. Now, the question is: Were these units on the following day really in their assigned areas of responsibility as defined in the order? I submit that all the evidence in the case, if interpreted correctly and if what I just mentioned is taken into account, all the evidence in the case, without exception, shows that all of these units were precisely where they were supposed to be. Not a single piece of evidence points to the contrary. I am absolutely convinced that the Viteska Brigade was in its own zone of responsibility, and I'm absolutely certain the others were too. What is the problem we faced in this case? In this case, Your Honours, during the Prosecution case, the OTP advanced the thesis, and I'm simplifying it now, that the HVO was equal to Cerkez. So whenever a witness said the HVO came in and did this or that, then the Prosecution interpreted this to mean Cerkez. Naturally, very soon in the trial other evidence emerged showing that the HVO was an organisation, was a party to the conflict, and that within that organisation in that area there were several discernible units of the HVO, none of which was the Viteska Brigade. Therefore, this thesis, and here I'm referring to the vagueness of the indictment, is not true. The HVO is not equal to Cerkez. The HVO had many brigades, and Cerkez was the commander of just one unit, which he has not denied from the very beginning. There were many exhibits in the trial showing that his brigade was established on the eve of the conflict. Therefore, this is another reason why this unit was not strong enough. Blaskic, as a commander, being aware of his forces, assigned just one limited sector to this unit. Therefore, this unit had a clearly defined area of responsibility. [In English] Your Honours, perhaps this would be a good moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you how long do you intend to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you give -- if you would be so kind to give me the opportunity to answer on that when you are coming back, because I cut out some things and will try to make an estimate. Otherwise, I could mislead you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this question immediately after the break. Normally your time would have elapsed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- but we'll discuss it only during the break. Only that the record is clear, Mr. Farrell, you indicated that the map shown on the ELMO was admitted into evidence during trial, that the record is clear. Can you also give us the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. Your Honour, it's my understanding as I suspected that the map that's been shown on the screen is the one that was agreed to by the parties and Your Honours for the purposes of the submissions. It's the copy of the map that was agreed to by the parties for the purpose of the appeal, and it was scanned into the record so that we could use it on the computer screens as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I can't remember the exhibit number we placed on it at the beginning of the hearing, but that's the one. If there isn't one, it might be advisable for the purpose of the record --

utterances.text: Your Honour. If I may assist, Your Honour. It is the very same map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's on the record. It's in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's 4 under annex 4 -- annex 6. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: None of the parties have a problem with this. I would kindly ask you to wind up in about 15 minutes. Would it be acceptable for you? We can continue on this basis. I think it's fair with respect to the time you missed. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope it won't be rude if I ask you for 20 minutes and, if you require, I can take up less time in my reply to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Minima non curat praetor. Therefore, the trial stands now adjourned until half past five, and you will have the requested 20 minutes. Thank you. The trial stays adjourned.

utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm confident that I could wrap that up in 20 minutes, as you kindly gave it to me. [Interpretation] First, my colleagues have warned me that perhaps some of the answers were not correct, the answers given to the question of Her Honour Judge Weinberg de Roca concerning the wedding. The wedding was announced and, as scheduled in the church records, two months ahead of the event. Witness Pranjes testified about this, and that can be found on page 26127 of the transcript. Next, His Honour Judge Schomburg mentioned the hours indicated in the duty-officer's logbook, and I think that what you quoted pertained to the 16th of April, whereas the page that I put on the screen had to do with the 15th of April. So a day before. I will now devote less than five minutes to the issue of responsibility under 7(1) and 7(3), and then five minutes will be devoted to Donja Veceriska and Stari Vitez, and then the last five minutes I will devote to our request, our proposal. As for the responsibility under 7(1) and 7(3), we believe that Cerkez should not have been found guilty for counts 5, 6, 14, 15, 17, 19, 29, 30, 31, 33, 35, 41, 42, 44 of the indictment, or rather, we believe that this pertains to all of the counts of which he was found guilty from count 5 through count 44, because, based on the judgement, Cerkez was found guilty under both Article 7(1) and 7(3). We base our submissions on the development of the jurisprudence. I will enumerate several judgements which state that cumulative convictions are not allowed, both under 7(1) and 7(3). This was stated in the following cases, and I would like to remind you that our judgement was passed down on the 27th of February, 2001. On the 20th of February, 2001, in Mucic case, paragraph 405; Kunarac case, the 12th of June, paragraph 173; Krstic trial judgement, 2nd of August, 2001, paragraph 65 -- 605; Naletilic judgement on the 31st of March, 2003, paragraph 79. The first two judgements that I mentioned, Kunarac and Mucic are appeals judgements, whereas the second two are trial judgements. Based on findings in these judgements, the Trial Chamber has to select which form of criminal responsibility is more appropriate for conviction. However, there can be no cumulative conviction. Now, five minutes to be devoted to Donja Veceriska. As regards the alleged attack on Donja Veceriska and the finding that Cerkez participated in that attack, based on which he acquired criminal responsibility, I would like to say the following: First of all, the unit of Cerkez was not present there. Two witnesses, one for the Prosecution and one for Defence, testified to this effect. One was Drmic Bono and the other one was Witness V. This is mentioned in my brief. In addition to that, there were documents reflecting that tensions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. between two communities existed there even before the attack. Their following acts which support the claim that this was a legitimate military objective. First of all, the village is located next to an important explosive factory, which is of great strategic importance. There were many exhibits corroborating this, so this is not disputed. Second, there was a military unit in the village, the military unit of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, defending the village. There were also village guards of Croats who were also defending their houses in the village. The fighting lasted for 48 hours, and on the second night of the fighting, both civilians and the soldiers, Bosniaks, left the village with the assistance of UNPROFOR. Only eight persons were killed in the fighting, and there is nothing to show whether these persons were civilians or soldiers and whether they were killed accidentally or whether they were killed as a result of excessive force. The configuration of terrain in the area of Kruscica [as interpreted] gave the possibility to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to use Kruscica as their stronghold in that area and to descend very easily to the area around the factory. Therefore, the HVO took the village precisely because they wanted to protect the explosive factory. And this is an important aspect. There was no evidence to show that the civilians who were killed during those 48 hours were disproportionate to the extent of the operation that was led there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Counsel warned me that there is an error in transcript in line 20, location Kruscica is mentioned instead of Donja Veceriska. We are talking now about Donja Veceriska. Sorry. In 21st line, in 20 line it's good. Kruscica, the soldiers to come to Donja Veceriska. Anyway, it's obvious. [Interpretation] As for Stari Vitez, the attack on Stari Vitez, it is claimed that the Viteska Brigade participated in that attack and Cerkez was found guilty of that. However, we claim that there was no evidence to show that, first of all, Viteska Brigade was involved in that attack, because, based on the orders that we showed you, it becomes obvious that that was not the area of responsibility assigned to Cerkez. Second, witnesses who could have given some details about the soldiers who were seen in Stari Vitez during the conflict said that those were either Vitezovi or members of police. Witness Zlotrg, at 1663, stated that Muslims were arrested there either by the military police or by Vitezovi. This is mentioned in my brief. Stari Vitez, similar to Donja Veceriska, was another stronghold of the forces of Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from October of 1992. The fact that Stari Vitez was encircled and that it mounted defensive operations for full 11 months. Therefore, this fact that they were encircled for 11 months shows that the HVO was never able to take Stari Vitez despite the fact that they made two attempts to do so. This is a fact that illustrates that here there were two armies. So the attack on Stari Vitez on the 16th of April was a justifiable military operation, and there is nothing to show that excessive disproportionate force was used against facilities in that location. Also, there is no evidence to show that civilian facilities were targeted. Basically, the HVO was thrown out of Stari Vitez as soon as the conflict broke out. I think that we were detailed enough in our brief regarding these issues. I would like now to put forward our proposals. So as to the first issue of Article 7(1) and 7(3), I believe them vital with respect to sentencing, obviously. If this Appeals Chamber accepts the jurisprudence we pointed to, Cerkez should not be convicted doubly, and I think that would evidently reduce his criminal responsibility and, subsequently, his sentence. As for other final submissions with regard to our submission that the Trial Chamber erroneously accepted the position that the conflict was international, if our arguments were to be accepted, counts 15, 19, 30, 31, 33, and 35 should be dropped, because it is acts under Article 2 of the Statute that are incriminated, and Article 2 does not apply if there is no international armed conflict. And as for the grounds of appeal to the effect that fair trial guarantees were violated in Cerkez's case, that would affect all counts, of course, and Cerkez should be acquitted on all of these counts. And as for a part of these convictions regarding the standard of findings, which should be the beyond reasonable doubt standard, Cerkez should be acquitted on counts 5, 6, 14, 15, 19, 41, and 42, because these findings conclude that Cerkez's units committed crimes in Stari Vitez, Donja Veceriska, and we believe there were not enough elements for such findings. As for the fourth ground of appeal, we are again dealing with the standard of beyond reasonable doubt. The situation is here as we indicated before, and with respect to sentencing, apart from the fact that I believe that counts 35 and 44 are indisputable, cumulative convictions should not be allowed under Article 7(1) and 7(3). And I submit that the Appeals Chamber should take a step-by-step approach. If our submission that the sentence is too high and should be reduced is accepted, then the Appeals Chamber should decide to what extent it should be reduced, in view of the grounds of appeal, and only as a second step, bearing in mind that counts 35 and 44 would be eliminated, since certain sessions already reduced the scope of other counts, and in view of the elimination of cumulative convictions, the Appeals Chamber should decide to what extent the sentence should be reduced with the elimination of these counts. Because, in that case, the responsibility of Cerkez should be significantly smaller. Certain facts were quoted regarding his family background as well, which clearly indicates that his sentence should be reduced, regardless of the ground of appeal. With this, I remain at your disposal for any questions, and I apologise for taking up more time than envisaged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were a number of issues raised by the appellant, counsel for the appellant Mr. Cerkez, and there were a number of references made in which counsel for the appellant informed you of the position and noted that it was in their brief. As a result, we will try and address our response in the following manner: There are a few issues that I will address and expect to be finished before the time runs out today. Those will be certain factual issues, one particular legal issue. I -- with leave of the Court, I will use the time I have to deal with the counts that the Pre-Appeal Judge had asked me whether there was any evidence on the record, the two counts that -- count 33 and count 41, and lastly, I will deal with, very briefly, the relationship between 7(3) and 7(1). Then my colleague Ms. Kind will deal with a few of the fair trial issues, the submission that they were unable to call Mr. Cerkez, the refusal to grant a delay in the brief, and maybe one other issue. And then Ms. Jarvis will speak for, I hope within 15 to 20 minutes, on international armed conflict and one comment on the persecution, the mens rea for persecution. There were a number of factual submissions in relation to fact, and the Court is fully aware of the standard required for review of factual submissions. There were some submissions about based on the fact that Mr. Cerkez had filed some information that he had to attend a wedding, which was called off at the last minute by a request by General Blaskic. There was some submissions as to how long it would take. I'm not sure that any of that information is on the record, but even accepting that it is, the standard that was set out in the Kunarac appeal must apply. The essential claim, the main claim that -- from which this emanated was the issue in relation to AT, and I made submissions yesterday in our brief, as I think relatively clear, I hope, on the issues of corroboration and the evidence that corroborates, and I won't repeat those. There was a comment about -- just one comment I want to respond to is the fact that there was a -- the war diary had a reference on the afternoon of the 15th and that the arrival of Mr. Cerkez was sometime after that, and that was corroborated by the war diary. First of all, in my respectful submission that certainly does not undermine AT's evidence, with all the corroborative evidence of AT, the fact that AT's evidence that he was at the meeting isn't reflected in the war diary. AT's testimony, as you will recall, is actually that he physically saw Cerkez after the meeting, that after he was told that there was the military meeting, Kraljevic and Cerkez came to his office, he saw him personally, that Cerkez asked for a particular weapon, a heavy machine-gun, because he was facing some difficulty, some of his -- the HVO was in Kruscica. And in the war diary there is corroborating evidence that Mr. Cerkez is fighting in Kruscica. The other aspect with respect to the war diary is that though the war diary records the meeting that's set out at 5.30, the war diary does not record a subsequent meeting between Cerkez and Blaskic. Now, if the appellant is going to fault the war diary on the basis that it should undermine AT's testimony, I note that the very diary he's relying on doesn't in fact have a notation of a subsequent meeting at around 6.30 between Cerkez and Blaskic. In relation to his comments regarding the evidence of AT, he spends a fair amount of time indicating that this is the evidence, essentially that the Trial Chamber then convicted, or this is at least the evidence that was crucial to the Trial Chamber's determination. At paragraph 688 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber sets out the particular role of Mario Cerkez. It limits it to April 1993. It refers to Vitez, Stari Vitez, Veceriska, and Ahmici, and then it goes through the evidence that the Trial Chamber lists in this section of the judgement regarding Mario Cerkez. At the end of this section, the Trial Chamber finds, in paragraph 703, that there is clear evidence that Mario Cerkez participated in the attacks on Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Veceriska. Then it sets out the information upon which the Trial Chamber relies, which is on the top of page 242. If you check those paragraphs from beginning to end and including the evidence that they rely on, they don't mention the testimony of Witness AT. They actually convict on the basis of the documentary evidence -- I'm sorry. They do infer his presence - my apologies - at the military meeting on the 15th of April, 1993. That's not correct. But they then refer to the documentary evidence and the entries in the duty-officer's log. When you go back through the preceding paragraphs, right through to the beginning of the section, there is no reference to the testimony of Witness AT. What they start with is the orders, and that's -- I'm going to just -- I'm referring to the judgement now, so it's at page 236. And they start with the orders that are listed there. There was other evidence that was before them that supported their conclusions, and there was other findings in the judgement that supported their conclusions. Without taking you to it, at paragraph 595 is the appointment of Cerkez as commander of the Vitez Brigade. At paragraph 596 there's testimony that his headquarters are in Vitez and that it's a territorially based brigade with special purpose units that are within the territorial zone and within the command structure, but that with respect to the Vitezovi, he was not in a position to command Kraljevic. There's reference at paragraph 599 regarding the mobilisation of 270 persons in three companies situated in various villages. And then at paragraph 599, there's a reference -- there's a reference on page 198. It's the end of paragraph 599. And this is in relation to the organisation of the brigade. The second-last sentence says: "Most significantly, a list of the 1st Battalion of the brigade, dated April the 14th, shows 270 personnel in three companies and situated in various villages." If I could ask the assistance of the clerk to put something on the ELMO. This is exhibit at trial Z653. And if you're able to read it, Your Honours, this is the document that's referred to in the second-last paragraph of 599 of the judgement. And it says: "List of personnel from the 1st Battalion." This is the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade. "Per village of deployment." And then if you look, you'll see such villages as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Nadioci, Santici, the 2nd Company has a number of villages, the 3rd Company, Gornja Veceriska, Stari Vitez. This is a list just of the 1st Battalion, not the other -- it was found by the Trial Chamber there were three battalions and there was evidence which was disputed by counsel but found by the Trial Chamber that there were three battalions. This one sets out as of the 14th. This is the day before the Trial Chamber finds that there's the meeting. This is the area that's in the responsibility of just the 1st Battalion, not his complete area. And you'll see that it says "Gornja Veceriska." You'll recall that on the 16th, Gornja Veceriska, the testimony of witness is that the civilians left Donja Veceriska to go to Gornja Veceriska, if I recall, and the Prosecution relied on that for the pending attack. There's a reference to Stari Vitez and there's a reference to Nadioci, Santici. The purpose of putting this before you is to let you see that the Court had relied on this and other evidence for the fact that they were organised in areas and that these were some of the areas that fall under their control and command. The Court also found that as a territorially based - sorry - territorially based unit it was responsible in Vitez and his headquarters were in the cultural centre in Vitez. We then go to the orders which are relied upon by the Trial Chamber, the ones that are at paragraph 689 at page 236. This lists a number of areas more expensive than the places I pointed out on the previous exhibit, because that was only the 1st Battalion. And if you look through it, it's quite evident that the orders that are issued by Colonel Blaskic to his direct subordinate - Mario Cerkez is the direct subordinate of Blaskic - you'll see the reference throughout to the same places: Donja Veceriska, which is listed many times; Ahmici; Stari Vitez; Sivrino Selo; and Vrhovine. I note one comment. If you notice on page 236, under (c) and under (d), there's a reference to Sivrino Selo. You may be aware of the fact that Witness AT testified that, when asked who was beside the military police in Ahmici, the unit that was beside the military police was the Vitez Brigade in Sivrino Selo. If you look at a map, you'll see that Sivrino Selo is right beside Pirici, and as you know, and as Defence counsel have indicated, Pirici was one of the villages, the small hamlets around Ahmici. So you have literally side by side, right beside Pirici and the next village is Sivrino Selo is the Vitez Brigade. They're not down only in Kruscica as the appellant would submit. If you then turn to page 237 of the judgement, this is a reference to Mario Cerkez's report to Blaskic. It says: "The town is clean, and we have about 50 Muslims in the cellar of the brigade police station." If I could ask the clerk for one minute. I just want to put another matter on the ELMO, please. I'll just ask you to recall the passage at the top of page 237 of the judgement. "The town is clean." The town - the Prosecution submission - is Vitez. That's what's referred to throughout in these documents. The town is Vitez. That's where his headquarters is, headquarters are. And then it says: "We have about 50 Muslims in the cellar of the brigade police station." If you look at the document on the screen, which is Exhibit Z2158, you'll see that the brigade police station is on the bottom right-hand side and it's 300 metres. You'll see the arrow to the cinema, which was Mario Cerkez's office. And this is in the town of Vitez. Now, if you read that in conjunction with the report, this is a report from Cerkez to Blaskic about the town being clean, that they have 50 Muslims in the cellar of the brigade police station, and then he says the word "we." He then says: "Stari Vitez still remains a problem. What shall we do?" The Prosecution's submission, the Trial Chamber was -- it was quite reasonable for the Trial Chamber to rely on this evidence to find that Mr. Cerkez was responsible and to reject the proposition that he was simply reporting on other units and other members of the HVO to assist Colonel Blaskic. If you also look at the war diary, on the 16th of April, there are 26 entries with the name Mario or Mario C or Cerkez, and there are seven entries on April 16th with the name of the Vitez Brigade. On the 17th, there are 21 entries under the name Mario and seven under the name Vitez Brigade. In the war diary on April 16th, at 11.20, there's a note of a person by the name of Marin S. calling M. Cerkez for -- and then there's some difficulty with the translation. It says: "Delivery of ammunition/support for Donja Veceriska." Also on April 16th, at 1.20 in the afternoon, once again there's a call to Mario Cerkez, asking: Did the guests arrive in Donja and Gornja Veceriska?" And then it says: "The guest arrived (of the Tvrtko Brigade)." You'll recall at 1.30 in the morning indicating that the Vitez Brigade was to operate with the Tvrtko Brigade. That and the other evidence of the reporting of Cerkez of the activity in Donja Veceriska, it's clear that he has responsibility for this area. The Court find in paragraph 696 of the evidence of his control over the troops and find that he has responsibility at paragraph 703. These findings are not dependent on the testimony of Witness AT. In fact, there's only one reference to his presence at the meeting on the 15th in this passage, in this part of judgement which sets out the role of Mario Cerkez. One thing to note about the common criminal plan, and Ms. Jarvis may speak more on the common criminal plan and his shared intent for the common criminal plan, but if you accept that he's found guilty under the common criminal plan and you accept that he's at the meeting, which the Trial Chamber did, then he's not -- his guilt should not have been limited to those areas where his troops are directly participating and there can be a demonstration of a direct link from him to the troops. The Court finds that his contribution is in relation to Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska. If that's his contribution to a common criminal plan, then he's responsible under the joint criminal enterprise liability for the acts of others. Therefore, if he was in attendance at the meeting on the 15th, and if the scope of the meeting covered Kraljevic, the military police, his activities, if that was the scope of the meeting and the scope of the shared common plan for persecution, then he actually got a benefit from the Trial Chamber limiting his liability to his direct participation, essentially finding him guilty under a common criminal plan for his direct participation under 7(1).

utterances.text: Thank you. Just to go back to the charges. The indictment refers, I think, to be fair, to the -- well, first of all, they are charged together. There was a second aspect to your question, Judge Guney. I'm sorry. I apologise. I've forgotten it.

If I can ask your indulgence for one minute, Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Guney. I was going to see whether I had any information as to what was set out in the pre-trial brief as well, but with your indulgence, I'll respond to that in the morning. That's in relation to --

utterances.text: If I just may add, also for tomorrow, that you could please be prepared to answer the question not only about the plan but also the scope of the plan and Mr. Cerkez's knowledge of the plan in detail, in particular, whether or whether not this plan also included acts of inhumane treatment, inhumane acts, and whether it included the alleged acts in relation to deprivation of liberty under Articles 2 and 5.
