utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. If I may move on to answering Your Honour's -- or at least the questions raised by the Pre-Trial Judge in terms of whether there's any evidence for count 33, which is the hostage-taking count, or count 41, which is the wanton destruction. Just before I approach -- before I address these issues, there was a question made to Ms. Brady, I think by Your Honour Judge Schomburg, about the extent to which you can rely on factual findings in the brief, essentially, and how do you determine whether or not there's been a factual finding that would be sufficient to warrant a conclusion that there's a finding to substantiate a conviction. The first step, obviously, is that -- the first step is where they've made clear factual findings. The second would be whether or not there are any other findings made by the Trial Chamber that would support the conclusions. Those would be the circumstances where there are findings of fact made, evidence accepted by the Trial Chamber, but it may be somewhere else in the brief and not referred specifically with respect to the count. The steps that the Court would have to take would be, and the Prosecution would submit, would be that where there are findings of fact in the judgement, in those circumstances where there are findings of fact by the Trial Chamber and where the application of the law, as accepted by the Trial Chamber, to those facts support their conclusions, then you have all the components that are in the judgement and that are not disputable and that would result in the conviction. The difficulty arises where there's -- there has to be a determination as to whether or not there have been findings of fact. And it would only be in those circumstances where, on the basis of the judgement, one could infer that the Court actually accepted the evidence as part of their facts, where you can infer from the subsequent findings later in the judgement, because, as we know, in this judgement there's often a recitation of the evidence and then a finding at the end. In those circumstances, I think it would -- the Court would have to clearly look at the judgement, determine whether or not the facts recited are the ones that are ultimately found and relied on, and in many of the instances here, the Trial Chamber actually indicated that it rejected the Defence case. So the inference left is that they accepted the Prosecution evidence which was recited and that's the basis of their conviction. Other than that, I think we'd run into some difficulty if we attempted to simply refer to the evidence, and I don't think that this Court is in a position to actually decide based on the evidence. That would be a de novo function which obviously this Court has already indicated it's not its function to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we all fully understand the way the judgement is written, and we have no common pattern of conduct how to write a judgement, and we have to accept the judgement as it is and to find whether or not it suffices. However, when I already asked you, as a follow-up question to Judge Guney's question, could you please be so kind and also tomorrow explain where in the judgement one can find certain elements of specific intent when it comes to persecutions. Where do we find these elements, and how were these elements pleaded during trial? I think this would be of assistance for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: We will endeavour to assist. Regarding count 33, then, on the basis of the understanding of the judgement and its findings, the elements are set out at paragraph 314, and the essence of the element is that when these -- it's for the detainees, when they're detained or they're taken as detainees, there's a threat to subject the detainees in this case, the language in paragraph 343 says"threatens to subject civilians who are unlawfully detained to inhumane treatment as the means of achieving the fulfilment of a condition." Now, the Trial Chamber has found that there was hostages -- sorry - a conviction for hostage-taking. And the evidence is found at paragraph 784. The question, if I understand it correctly from the Pre-Appeal Judge, was to determine whether there was any evidence to substantiate the conviction for hostage-taking for prisoners in the detention centres beyond the Vitez cinema. If you -- if I may take you to paragraph 784, subparagraph (b), the evidence relied upon was that Mr. Cerkez had asked a detainee, a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prominent Muslim doctor, Mujezinovic, to call upon the ABiH to stop attacking. Now, this commission that was to be set up to call upon the ABiH to stop attacking was in the Vitez cinema, but in the Prosecution's submission, this relates to all the detainees in all the detention centres in Vitez. The sentence goes on and says: "That there will be a call upon the ABiH to stop attacking or all prisoners held in Vitez would be killed." Not simply the prisoners that are detained in the Vitez cinema where this takes place. If I may take you over to paragraph 788, subparagraph (viii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand your conclusion, and it will be for the Chamber to decide whether this suffices in relation to the veterinary station, the SDK offices, and the Chess Club. However, is it your submission that it's enough to say detainees, without specific elaboration on the question whether these detainees were military persons or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In light of the fact that it's a threat to treat them inhumanely, the threat to kill would obviously satisfy that regardless, I would submit, of the status. At paragraph 788, subparagraph (viii), there's further evidence that, according to Dr. Mujezinovic, Mario Cerkez had told him that the ABiH had broken through the front line at Dubravica. Once again, the witness had to call the 3rd Corps commander, the 3rd Corps commander is the ABiH army, and say that if the Muslim advance continued on Vitez, he would order the killing of the prisoners. The witness, Dr. Mujezinovic, did so, did phone the 3rd Corps of the ABiH army, and the commander agreed to halt the advance. Now, this is corroborative evidence, if it may, or additional evidence of a separate incident in which the threat was for all prisoners, and it's submitted that the inference is clear that it comes from -- well, it comes from Mario Cerkez and the inference is clear it's those prisoners that he is able to kill. Those are the two findings of fact I could refer you to that may, if the Court so decides, substantiate the charge of count 33, hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In addition, 788.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Correct. Detention of Muslims. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was already clarified in the past, but what about 31? I think it was conceded that there were made no factual findings relating to the involvement of forces under Mr. Cerkez's responsibility in Stari Vitez and Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. It is clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The other one that the Court had asked was count 41, for Mr. Cerkez, wanton destruction, and the question, as I recall, was in relation to Vitez and Stari Vitez. Now, the judgement sets out, at paragraph 8071, for this count of wanton destruction, Vitez and Stari Vitez, 807, sub(i) and sub(ii). I think it's fairly clear that 807 sub(i) refers to a period of time in October 1992 and early 1993, but doesn't specifically refer to April 1993, which is the period of time for which Mr. Cerkez was convicted. In relation to Stari Vitez, which is the next subparagraph, once again, there does not appear, on the face of it, to be specific factual findings in relation to the HVO, Vitez Brigade, and Stari Vitez in April 1993. There is other evidence on the record that I want to bring to your attention, which I leave it to the Court to determine whether it's sufficient to warrant the conviction, but I'll inform you of what evidence is on the record in this regard. For Vitez, for wanton destruction, there is evidence in the unlawful attack section of the judgement where, though referring to the unlawful attack section, they actually refer to the results of the unlawful attack, which, in the Prosecution's submission, there are some factual findings regarding the destruction. In paragraph 644, there is reference to Colonel Watters' testimony. Now, before I refer to it, Judge Schomburg, you asked a question of my learned friend about whether Vitez and Stari Vitez were included in the same. I agree with the Defence counsel, Vitez includes Stari Vitez as a geographical area. I think the reason that -- in the indictment was because they at one point in time became separate communities, in light of the fact that Stari Vitez was controlled by the ABiH and Vitez was under the HVO control. And here, when they're referring to it, they don't distinguish specifically it in the evidence, though they talk about the Muslim part of Vitez. In paragraph 643, there is the evidence of Colonel Watters that he had received reports of shelling and firing on Muslim areas of Kruscica and Vitez and that, based on his observations, he came to the opinion that most of the destruction and casualties were in the Muslim area of the town. There also is reference to Exhibit 2007, support of this in footnote 1247. Footnote 1247 lists Colonel Watters' testimony and the corroborative evidence of smoke and fires and bodies lying on the far side of Vitez, also that there are a number of bodies in Stari Vitez. The only other evidence that I could locate, Your Honours, is that Witness TW21 from the Blaskic trial is referred to in footnote 1251, and the testimony, I'm being very specific here, because I'm trying to identify the specific - the testimony referred to from 4471 to 4474 relates to the sexual assault and the jewellery. She also testified to a number of Muslim houses burning in Vitez. But that testimony of the Muslim houses burning in Vitez is two pages earlier. It's at 4476. Sorry. Two pages later. Those are the three pieces of evidence that I could locate that appears to have been accepted by the Trial Chamber, in which there were factual findings and evidence relied upon in relation to destruction in Vitez and/or Stari Vitez. There may be one other question that arises from this, which is -- I think the Court hasn't asked about the link evidence of the HVO being in Vitez, or Stari Vitez, but in light of the fact that Mr. Kovacic has indicated that, I would note that the Trial Chamber accepted the testimony in paragraph 644 of Mr. Breljas that the Vitez Brigade took part in the attack in Stari Vitez, and there was also evidence which was accepted by the Court in relation to the detention crimes that some of the witnesses who testified and their evidence was accepted in relation to the detention crimes, some of those witnesses identified Vitez Brigade members as the HVO members who arrested them in Vitez on April 16th. That would be particularly witness Fuad Zeko, who testified that there were two members who arrested him on the 16th of April, at 6.00 in the morning. One of the members -- one of the persons who arrested him is named Krunoslav Bonic. And the linkage that is found is that the Trial Chamber actually accepted a list of exhibits setting out all the members of the brigade. That's Exhibit Z1337.1. It's referred to in footnote 1097. They also accepted, in footnote 1114, a file put forward by the Prosecution as Exhibit Z2813.2, both which indicate that this individual who appeared at the house of Mr. Zeko and arrested him and took him to the veterinarian station and detained him, this was a member of the Vitez Brigade. There's also testimony of Witness G, which was testimony in closed session, that this person was taken to the cultural centre on April 19th. The Trial Chamber relied on the testimony of this witness in paragraph 788, subparagraph 2 of the judgement, related to his evidence regarding his detention in the cinema. And he identifies an individual by the name of Boro Jozic in that -- in those passages, and once again, the list that the Trial Chamber refers to in footnote 1097, Exhibit Z1337.1, lists Mr. Boro Jozic as a member of the command of the Viteska Brigade. That's the evidence that I was able to identify for the purposes of Vitez, Stari Vitez, on the 16th to the 19th of April. In relation to the question by the Pre-Trial Judge of the relationship between 7(1) and 7(3) and the submission by my learned friend in that regard, I note that the jurisprudence starting with Blaskic, if I recall - I don't have the passage; I apologise - has attempted to deal with this overlap between 7(1) and 7(3). You'll recall that in the Krstic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found that though the elements were met, it exercised its discretion not to enter a conviction. In the Krnojelac trial, the Trial Chamber exercised the same discretion and indicated that the conduct or criminality of the accused was better characterised under 7(1). If the criminal conduct that -- if -- I'm sorry. If 7(1) and 7(3) are based on the exact same criminal conduct, there may technically be a conviction in that there was both the order to commit the crime and then the failure to punish or even prevent or punish afterwards. But, with respect to, if it's the same conduct, it, at least at first blush, it doesn't appear to make sense that you would convict him twice for ordering a crime and then convict him again for failing to prevent his own order. And in that regard, I think that if there's direct involvement by the commander under 7(1), his conduct would be -- though technically he would be found guilty on both, the conviction would be better characterised as 7(1), if that's the circumstance, in my respectful submission. Those, essentially, are the matters I wanted to submit to the Court in response to the comments by my friend, with the exception of one. There was a submission made, if I recall, on the forging of a particular document. I think it's 692, sub(3), if I recall. I'll make one quick submission. This matter, as I understand, was raised before the Trial Chamber, and this matter was addressed. The document fits in a line of documents which the Court accepted as demonstrating its consistency. The fact that it's a copy isn't determinative of admissibility or not. Obviously there's a number of document, most documents that we get from state parties are copies. The question has to be whether or not it's a document that meets admissibility requirements under 89(C). The fact that a party objects in and of itself doesn't make a document inadmissible. The court still has a make a determination. If the logic is extended that if a party objects then the other party has to demonstrate its authenticity. Mr. Cerkez is relying on the war diary. Mr. Kordic has objected to it. So I guess Mr. Cerkez would have to actually demonstrate the authenticity of the war diary to rely on it, because Mr. Cerkez has objected to it. I don't think that would be the approach that the Trial Chamber would have taken and they would have looked at the document in light of all the other documents and determined whether or not it was accepted. Other than that and the questions which I hope to be in a position to answer tomorrow morning by Your Honour Judge Guney and Your Honour Judge Schomburg, those are the submissions of the Prosecution on the factual errors, the counts that the Court had asked us on, and the position on 7(1) and 7(3). We're either in a -- well, it may not make a lot of sense to continue at this time, but I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, in fact, it makes not much sense to continue with another chapter for today, so we will continue tomorrow at 9.00 sharp, and hope that we can conclude, as scheduled, tomorrow. The trial stays adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
